The optimal formulation (24 wt% Dex, 14 wt% MD, and 0.24 wt% BCNCs) exhibited a uniform droplet distribution and enhanced storage stability. Contact angle analysis indicated preferential wettability of BCNCs toward the continuous Dex-rich phase, promoting interfacial adsorption and droplet stabilization. The emulsions remained stable at pH 3.0-7.0 but were sensitive to ionic strength above 7 mM sodium chloride. Importantly, in vitro digestion showed that BCNC-stabilized emulsions significantly inhibited α-amylase-mediated hydrolysis of AMP, with the hydrolysis extent reducing from ~54% to 14%. These results indicate that BCNCs act as effective natural stabilizers for W/W Pickering emulsions, forming a physical barrier that retards starch digestion. This work provides a sustainable strategy for designing slow-digestible, low-glycemic-index food systems with potential applications in functional foods and pharmaceuticals.
doi:10.3390/foods15132401: This study developed a pH-responsive dual-network polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) active packaging film by integrating cellulose nanocrystal (CNC)-stabilized Mosla chinensis essential oil (EO) emulsions with a tannic acid-Fe 3+ metal-phenolic network (MPN). The CNC-stabilized emulsion improved EO dispersion and retention in the PVA matrix and contributed to network reinforcement through hydrogen-bonding interactions, while the dynamic MPN further strengthened the film structure and acted as a pH-gated domain for regulating EO release. Composite film achieved high UVA and UVB blocking efficiencies of 90.06% and 99.60%, respectively, together with improved mechanical, barrier, antioxidant, and antibacterial properties. Compared with neutral conditions (pH = 7), EO release increased by 179.9% and 181.3% at pH = 4 and pH = 9, respectively, confirming the pH-gated release behavior of the film. In yam preservation, composite film effectively delayed browning, weight loss, firmness decline, and spoilage. Metabolomic analysis further indicated that the film treatment regulated phenylpropanoid metabolism and flavonoid biosynthesis, which may contribute to maintaining antioxidant-related metabolic homeostasis. This work offers a pH-responsive controlled-release active packaging strategy for browning-prone fresh produce.
doi:10.1167/iovs.67.8.19: Purpose The purpose of this study was to quantitatively determine the intrinsic evaporation resistance of the tear film lipid layer (TFLL) and resolve discrepancies between in vivo and in vitro findings. Methods A controlled-area droplet evaporimeter (CADE) was developed based on constrained drop surfactometry. The system integrates three independent feedback control loops to maintain constant droplet surface area, surface temperature (34°C), and environmental relative humidity (30%-70%). A model TFLL composed of representative polar and nonpolar lipids was studied. Evaporation flux was measured under controlled interfacial conditions at defined surface pressures. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) was used to characterize TFLL lateral structure and topography. Results CADE enabled direct quantification of TFLL evaporation resistance under physiologically relevant conditions. Evaporation resistance increased significantly with surface pressure, from approximately 11% at 20 mN/m to approximately 37% at 35 mN/m, consistent with values reported in vivo. In contrast to a pure air-water surface exhibiting diffusion-limited evaporation, TFLL-covered surfaces displayed interface-limited behavior, indicating that the lipid layer introduces a dominant transport resistance. AFM revealed a concurrent structural transition from heterogeneous nonpolar lipid lenses to a more uniform and continuous dual-layered film with increasing surface pressure. Conclusions The TFLL provides a substantial and surface pressure-dependent barrier to evaporation, governed by interfacial organization rather than thickness. By isolating intrinsic TFLL properties, CADE reconciles discrepancies between in vivo and in vitro measurements and establishes a mechanistic framework linking lipid organization to evaporation resistance. This platform offers new opportunities for studying tear film biophysics and for developing lipid-based therapies for evaporative dry eye disease (DED).
doi:10.1039/d6ra02776h: Soft actuators aim to bridge the gap between rigid machines and soft matter by mimicking the flexibility and compliance of natural muscles and tissues. Stimuli-responsive hydrogels can fit this purpose through their softness and ability for large reversible shape morphing. However, the performance of hydrogel actuators is restricted by their diffusion-limited water transport, which leads to slow responses, and uniform volumetric changes that generate limited actuation forces and strains. Thus, there is a need to develop faster hydrogel actuators that can efficiently convert swelling into actuation force and strain. Anisotropic cellulose nanofibril (CNF) hydrogels offer a route to overcome these limitations by assembling charged fibrils into dense, layered sheets that are reinforced in-plane while remaining compliant in the thickness direction. This architecture redirects water uptake into uniaxial expansion or, under confinement, into high blocking pressure, thereby combining large strain, high force, and rapid response. Here, we establish how the structure and processing of charged CNF networks govern swelling-driven actuation. Specifically, we examine how fibril properties, including aspect ratio and charge density, together with sheet fabrication parameters, including drying conditions and actuator area, control the translation of water uptake into directional strain and force. Optimization of these parameters results in CNF networks that expand uniaxially by 220 times within an hour with initial strain rates of 190-300% s -1 , reaching blocking pressures up to 4.9 MPa in less than a minute. These hydrogels are a great step towards hydrogel-based artificial muscles, which have been prevented by the slow response of previously reported stimuli-responsive hydrogels. Further development of fibrillar hydrogel actuators can lead to truly lifelike artificial muscles.
doi:10.1088/1361-6501/aebb53: Abstract Thermal calibration of atomic force microscopy (AFM) cantilever spring constant, k, is routinely performed by fitting the thermal displacement power spectral density (PSD) to a simple harmonic oscillator (SHO) model. Experiments performed in liquid present the choice of whether to also calibrate in liquid or to pre-calibrate in air, where reduced hydrodynamic drag produces a sharper resonance peak. It remains an open question whether this yields a more accurate calibration. Here we use a hydrodynamic model introduced by Sader and later extended by Bellon to generate thermal PSDs for two cantilevers of differing known stiffness across four media of increasing viscosity. We then fit each generated PSD with the SHO model used in experimental calibration (under various parameters and conditions). Iteratively fitting in the vicinity of the resonance peak, with logarithmic weighting and a fitted noise term, recovers the known spring constant to within 3% in every medium including the most viscous, where the fundamental mode of the softer cantilever is overdamped. We use this analysis to identify an optimal fitting strategy-in terms of window size, window center, and weighting-for experimentally reasonable cantilever properties and describe a general procedure for determining these parameters for other cantilevers. We show that the optimal fit-window width is not universal but can be determined for any cantilever and medium by applying the same analysis with different parameters. To confirm these results, we experimentally calibrated the same two types of cantilevers in air and liquid and obtained k values that agreed closely, despite several-fold changes in resonance frequency and quality factor upon immersion. These results demonstrate that AFM cantilevers intended for liquid-phase measurements can be reliably calibrated in situ, without recourse to a separate calibration in air.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11212419/v1: Abstract Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits an intricate and multifactorial pathogenesis. Existing research on amyloid-β (Aβ)-triggered neurotoxicity has predominantly centered on neuronal apoptosis, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial damage. The role of biomechanical signaling, a vital regulatory mechanism in neuronal physiological homeostasis and AD pathological progression, remains largely uncharacterized in the context of Aβ-mediated neurotoxicity. Here, differentiated SH-SY5Y, neuron-like cells, were used to examine the Aβ42 oligomers induced cellular mechanics alteration and the abnormal activation of mechanosensitive ion channels. Aβ42 oligomer adsorption increases cellular Young's modulus, which is associated with sustained intracellular Ca 2+ elevation mediated by Piezo1. Subsequently, the overloaded Ca 2+ induces mitochondrial dysfunction, excessive reactive oxygen species accumulation, YAP/TAZ signaling activation, cytoskeletal remodeling, dynamic changes in cellular stiffness, and finally a cell death through caspase-4-mediated non-canonical pyroptosis. These findings support an Aβ42-Piezo1-Ca 2+ -cytoskeletal remodeling axis that links altered neuronal mechanics to neurotoxicity and identify Piezo1 as a potential target for further investigation in AD.
doi:10.1002/snz2.70090: This review examines the current literature on the application of atomic force microscopy (AFM) to cancer mechanophenotyping, with particular emphasis on cellular Young's modulus and its potential diagnostic significance. A structured electronic search of PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar was conducted to identify studies published between 1999 and 2025 reporting AFM-based measurements of cellular Young's modulus in cancer-related models. Across multiple malignancies, reduced cellular stiffness is frequently observed in malignant compared with non-malignant cells and is associated with cytoskeletal remodelling, increased deformability and altered cell-matrix interactions. However, the relationship between Young's modulus and malignancy is not universally monotonic. Nanomechanical properties may vary across different pathological states and malignant phenotypes rather than following a simple monotonic trajectory, while invasive and metastatic cells can dynamically remodel their cytoskeleton and modify their stiffness in response to environmental and mechanical constraints. Young's modulus should therefore not be regarded as an isolated universal cancer biomarker, but rather as one component of a dynamic mechanophenotype influenced by disease stage, cellular region, microenvironment and measurement methodology. Recent advances in automated force acquisition, optical cell recognition, artificial intelligence and high-throughput AFM are beginning to address traditional limitations in measurement efficiency and operator dependence. The future diagnostic value of AFM may therefore lie in integrating Young's modulus with complementary parameters, including spatial mechanical heterogeneity, viscoelasticity, adhesion, deformation-energy characteristics and nanotopography, to define multidimensional cancer mechanophenotypes. Standardised acquisition and analysis protocols, together with validation in patient-derived specimens, will be essential for translating AFM nanomechanics from an experimental measurement into a clinically informative biomechanical biomarker.
doi:10.1002/app.71654: ABSTRACT Ethylene‐propylene‐diene monomer (EPDM) rubber relies on plasticizers for flexibility and processability; however, conventional petrochemical oils pose significant environmental challenges. This study investigates a commercially available bio‐based oil as a partial or full replacement for fossil‐based paraffinic oil in EPDM formulations. Compounds containing purely bio‐based or purely conventional oil exhibited similar mechanical properties, although the bio‐based variant showed slightly reduced thermo‐oxidative aging resistance. Blends with 25% and 75% bio‐based oil fractions yielded modest increases in tensile strength (5% and 16%, respectively), as well as increased stiffness and crosslink density, indicating good compatibility. In contrast, the 50% blend initially displayed poorer mechanical performance. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) linked this behavior to a specific phase morphology, even though the compound retained notable tear resistance. After tempering, particularly at 70°C, the mechanical properties of the 50% blend improved to levels comparable or better than the other variants. Temperature Scanning Stress Relaxation (TSSR) confirmed that these changes were likely rooted in rearrangements of the sulfur network. Notably, the tensile strength of this blend reached its peak after aging, showing a 35% increase compared to the unaged reference. These results suggest that phase morphology influences the distribution of curing chemicals.
doi:10.1002/smtd.71106: Mechanical characterization of 3D printed hydrogel microstructures typically relies on invasive, contact-based methods that are challenging to perform in aqueous environments. Here, we present a fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM)-based approach that exploits the intrinsic autofluorescence of two-photon 3D laser-printed hydrogel microstructures to enable label- and contact-free mechanical mapping. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based micropillar arrays are fabricated with systematically varied laser doses to modulate the degree of network crosslinking, thereby tuning the material stiffness. FLIM measurements reveal a monotonic increase in the intensity-averaged autofluorescence lifetime with increasing laser dose, reflecting a concomitant increase in stiffness. To quantify the mechanical properties of the 3D printed microstructures in aqueous media, we develop a buoyancy-corrected nanoindentation protocol. The resulting reduced moduli exhibit the same trend and show strong agreement with the fluorescence lifetime measurements. In addition, the autofluorescence signal of the micropillars proved highly sensitive to changes in the hydration state. Thus, these results demonstrate that FLIM is a powerful, noninvasive tool for high-resolution mechanical mapping of soft materials, particularly in conditions where other more conventional methodologies are challenging.
doi:10.1007/s10439-026-04420-2: PURPOSE: Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) is an established technique to measure the mechanical properties of cells and tissues. Measurements are based on force interactions between cantilever and sample. These measurements can be influenced by the underlying substrate. Published literature has utilized this phenomenon to measure the turgor pressure of eukaryotic cells through the cell membrane. The purpose of the current study was to determine how to increase measurement sensitivity of pressure in larger-scale biological tissues, specifically intraocular pressure. METHODS: AFM was used to measure pressurized artificial corneas. Tipless and tipped cantilevers were used to acquire measurements of Young's modulus of elasticity and apparent stiffness over the pressure range: 15, 25, and 35 mmHg to represent normal, elevated, and uncontrolled IOP. RESULTS: In this study, fourteen tipless cantilevers and eight modified cantilevers were tested to determine which cantilever parameters best measured the pressure beneath the tissue. The parameters evaluated were spring constant, indenter tip radius, and effective working length. Spring constant had a more pronounced effect on apparent stiffness than any other parameter examined for both unmodified and modified cantilevers. For modified cantilevers, the ratio of working length to indenter radius enhances the bottom-substrate effect, with lower ratios being more advantageous. CONCLUSION: The results of this study suggest that AFM could be used to quantify pressure beneath biological tissues, but care must be taken to select a cantilever with appropriate specifications.
doi:10.1002/pola.70375: ABSTRACT Epoxy/thermoplastic blends often undergo reaction‐induced phase separation (RIPS) during curing, and introducing a deformable thermoplastic component is generally expected to improve the deformation tolerance of brittle epoxy networks. In this study, hydroxyl‐terminated oligomeric poly(phenylene ether) (oPPE) was introduced into an epoxy/amine system to clarify how an initially optically homogeneous formulation evolves into a hierarchically phase‐separated network and how the resulting oPPE‐rich morphology affects tensile ductility. Before curing, no optically detectable macroscopic phase separation was observed in the bisphenol‐A diglycidyl ether (DGEBA)/oPPE mixtures, whereas curing produced a hierarchical phase‐separated morphology consisting of primary oPPE‐rich domains and nanoscale secondary subdomains, which is consistent with a two‐stage RIPS scenario. Synchrotron X‐ray scattering, thermal relaxation, and atomic force microscopy nanomechanics confirmed the multiscale structural and local mechanical heterogeneity. Despite this hierarchical morphology, tensile ductility decreased with increasing oPPE content. Fracture‐surface observations revealed interfacial gaps and cavities around the primary domains, suggesting that primary domain–matrix debonding contributes significantly to the reduced tensile ductility and overall failure process.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11077305/v1: Abstract Thermal transport in coal governs conversion efficiency in gasification, coking and combustion, yet established methods need machined or compacted specimens and return bulk values in which intrinsic conduction, porosity and contact resistance are inseparable. Here, optothermal Raman (OTR) thermometry is applied to individual as-received grains of anthracite, semi-anthracite and lignite, combined on the same grains with five-band micro-Raman deconvolution, SEM-EDS and AFM surface and nanomechanical mapping; bulk proximate analysis and the ASTM D388 rank classification give an independent reference. The G-band temperature coefficient, calibrated between 293 and 873 K, was χ G = − 0.0328 ± 0.0033, − 0.0098 ± 0.0033 and − 0.0333 ± 0.0033 cm − 1 K − 1 , and a power ramp from 5 to 20 mW (to 15 mW for lignite) gave Δω G /Δ P = − 0.514 ± 0.099, − 0.500 ± 0.041 and − 0.300 ± 0.058 cm − 1 mW − 1 . A steady-state solution for a 590 nm source on a semi-infinite absorbing solid gave effective grain conductivities of 17.2 ± 3.7, 5.3 ± 1.8 and 29.9 ± 6.5 W m − 1 K − 1 , one to two orders of magnitude above bulk coal values and within the optothermal-Raman range for low-ordered carbon fibers. Across the series the G-band width narrowed from 69.24 to 53.11 cm − 1 , the O/C ratio fell from 0.343 to 0.066 and dry, mineral-matter-free fixed carbon from 96.60 to 51.37%. The G-band width varied linearly with both surface O/C and bulk volatile matter, and contact-potential dispersion widened from 50.9 µV to 369 mV. The protocol yields preparation-free, spatially resolved thermal and structural descriptors of carbonaceous fuels.
doi:10.1038/s42004-026-02229-7: Abstract Polymer grafts are a ubiquitous component of nanocrystal (NC) ligand shells and impart critical functionalities, including biocompatibility and colloidal stability. Although many techniques have been used for elucidating the supramolecular structure of polymer chains once grafted to the NC surface, few of these are able to provide a complete picture of the ligand shell under experimentally relevant conditions ( e.g ., low polymer densities, various solvent environments). Here, we use high-resolution atomic force microscopy imaging along with coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to directly image polymers grafted onto single Ag NCs in both air and water to better understand the ligand-solvent interactions that dictate ligand shell structuring. For hydrophobic grafts under poor solvent conditions, the grafts self-associate to form a patchy shell, as previously reported. However, for hydrophilic grafts under good solvent conditions, this patchy morphology persists and is observed even for polyethylene glycol-functionalized NCs (i.e. PEGylated) in water. Polymer structuring is also observed amongst assembled NCs, with the formation of polymer bridges forming across patches. These unexpected results suggest that surface patchiness may be more widespread in colloidal NC systems than previously assumed, and this surface heterogeneity could play an important role in governing collective NC phenomena such as self-assembly.
doi:10.1016/j.colsurfb.2026.116252: Candida albicans (C. albicans) is a commensal member of the oral microbiota that can form biofilms, contributing to denture stomatitis. Its initial adhesion to abiotic surfaces is a critical step in biofilm formation and is strongly influenced by the material's physicochemical properties. Surface roughness, surface free energy (SFE), and salivary components play key roles in mediating fungal-material interactions. Polymeric materials are components of denture materials, so understanding the interactions with C. albicans is essential to clarify the mechanisms underlying early fungal adhesion. However, the molecular and biophysical mechanisms that govern fungal adhesion to polymer materials are not well characterized. This study examined C. albicans adhesion behavior on polyvinyl chloride (PVC) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) surfaces with defined roughness levels Ra = 0.2 μm and 0.04 μm) with saliva. Surface properties were characterized using profilometry and contact angle measurements, while adhesion forces and cell-surface interactions were analyzed by single-cell force spectroscopy (SCFS) using atomic force microscopy (AFM) varying contact forces. The expression of the adhesion- and biofilm-associated genes ALS1, HWP1, and EFG1 was quantified by quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR). Rough surfaces resulted in stronger adhesion and more contact points. In contrast, higher SFE was associated with reduced adhesion. Saliva pretreatment modulated these interactions. Gene expression analyses revealed that early adhesion is primarily regulated by polymer-dependent surface signals, while hyphae- and biofilm-specific pathways exhibited minimal activation. In summary, the results demonstrate that the surface properties of polymeric materials significantly influence the early adhesion of C. albicans and its associated molecular responses.
doi:10.1111/jmi.70183: AFM is not for the faint of heart. It has never been for these 40 years since its invention or for any of the modalities that have emerged. And among them, the initial concept of using AFM to measure cell mechanics was simply brazen. On the one hand, those pioneers hacked an imaging tool optimised for minimal mechanical interaction between probe and sample, and used it to locally indent living cells. On the other hand, they did so to measure stiffness of cells, a feature that no one in the cell biology or biomedicine communities gave relevance to or even credit. Through their total disregard for the status quo, they helped establish two topics that today employ thousands of researchers worldwide: AFM for nanomechanical mapping of soft samples, and the research field of mechanobiology.
doi:10.3389/frlct.2026.1968871: Cancer progression is shaped by coupled molecular, biochemical, and mechanical changes across multiple scales, from altered signaling and cytoskeletal organization to cellular deformation, adhesion, and metastatic dissemination. Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are rare and heterogeneous in blood, occurring as single cells and multicellular clusters that provide access to evolving tumor phenotypes through liquid biopsy. Their apparent elasticity, deformability, adhesion, and viscoelastic behavior may reflect invasive potential, treatment response, and phenotypic state, while cytoskeletal proteins, membrane lipids, cell surface glycans, and receptors provide molecular context for these mechanical signatures. This review examines the complementary roles of microfluidics and atomic force microscopy (AFM) in multiscale CTC mechanobiology. Microfluidic platforms support label-free and affinity-based enrichment, capture, positioning, and recovery of viable cells. AFM provides localized measurements of apparent elasticity, deformation, adhesion, viscoelastic response, and nanoscale surface architecture in liquid, while functionalized probes enable molecular recognition and molecule-specific force measurements. We evaluate physical, affinity-based, cluster-preserving, open-space, and artificial intelligence-assisted microfluidic strategies together with reversible device assembly, automated AFM targeting, fluidic probes, advanced mapping modes, and treatment-response applications. Existing studies establish feasibility, including direct AFM measurements of individual patient-derived CTCs and automated analysis following microfluidic enrichment in model rare-cell mixtures. Clinical evidence remains limited, many integrated workflows rely on cultured cells or spiked samples, and within the literature identified in this review, direct AFM characterization of intact patient-derived CTC clusters was not found. Clinical translation will require confirmation of tumor identity, standardized acquisition, analysis, and reporting, increased throughput, statistical analysis that preserves the hierarchy of patients, cells, and force curves, and validation in independent patient cohorts. Integrated AFM-microfluidic platforms could extend CTC liquid biopsy beyond enumeration toward functional mechanobiological analysis relevant to metastasis, therapeutic response, and biomarker development.
doi:10.1029/2026gl122474: Abstract Particle size and physical properties such as stiffness and adhesiveness affect sinking velocity and flux in the ocean, yet conventional two‐dimensional measurements lack accuracy and mechanical information. In this study, we applied atomic force microscopy (AFM) to quantify three‐dimensional size and physical properties of marine particles. Three hundred and sixty‐eight particles were collected using a marine snow catcher from the pycnocline and benthic boundary layer at three coastal‐to‐offshore stations in the northwestern Pacific. Particle equivalent spherical diameters (ESDs) ranged from 0.4 to 32 μm, with >70% smaller than 10 μm. Two‐dimensional analyses overestimated ESDs of settled particles by ∼1.5 times (∼3.3 times in volume) relative to three‐dimensional measurements. Young's modulus (0.07–616 MPa) and adhesiveness (331–2,802 pN) varied widely and overlapped reported values for bacteria, diatoms, and mucus. Particle physical properties differed systematically with depth and location, indicating that AFM provides critical constraints on particle dynamics, origins, and marine biogeochemical cycles.
doi:10.1021/acs.macromol.6c02167: Abstract Understanding the interactions between polymers and inorganic fillers is crucial for enhancing interfacial effects and optimizing the mechanical properties of polymer nanocomposites. We used two atomic force microscopy (AFM)-based nanomechanical techniques: nanomechanical AFM mapping and single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS), to quantitatively characterize the adhesion between polymers and inorganic materials from the aggregate scale to the single-chain scale. This study reveals the relationship between single-molecule interactions and adhesion behavior at the aggregate scale by comparing the interactions between cis-1,4-polyisoprene (PI) monolayers and inorganic substrates with the adhesion between inorganic-coated probes and cross-linked isoprene rubber (IR). In addition, SMFS measurements reveal solvent-dependent adsorption conformations and substrate-dependent desorption forces, enabling quantitative analysis of adsorption at the molecular scale. For PI, which lacks strongly interacting polar functional groups, nonspecific van der Waals-dominated interactions are expected to contribute substantially to its interactions with the inorganic substrates. The observed substrate dependence reflects differences in interfacial characteristics, including surface free energy. Furthermore, by measuring the adhesion energy at the PI aggregate scale via nanomechanical AFM mapping using surface-modified probes, the results revealed a trend similar to that observed in a single polymer chain. This cross-scale consistency highlights substrate surface characteristics as important factors regulating polymer–inorganic interfacial interactions. This research methodology provides an effective strategy for rational design of interface interactions and lays a theoretical foundation for structural optimization and performance enhancement of high-performance polymer composites.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10759060/v1: Abstract Single-cell force spectroscopy is a vital technique for studying mechanobiology, with traditional indentation methods primarily assessing the static bulk resistance of the cytoplasm. In this study, we introduce nanoscale dynamic force spectroscopy (Nano-DFS), a label-free physical method that captures the states of live cells. By analyzing velocity dependent force spectroscopy of membrane nanotube tethers across a range of pulling velocities, Nano-DFS quantitatively extracts dynamic mechanical features at the membrane interface. Using breast cancer cell lines, we demonstrated that nanotether dynamics can effectively distinguish between different cell types. We validated this method under physiological and pharmacological conditions, showing that these dynamic signatures are sensitive physical indicators that differentiate non-tumorigenic cells from invasive phenotypes. Ultimately, Nano-DFS offers a robust, non-genetic approach to directly examine the physical architecture of live cells and to track dynamic cell states during disease progression or therapeutic intervention.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.01.756136: Abstract Centromeric heterochromatin is maintained by a self-reinforcing loop between DNA methylation (5mC) and histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), yet whether this coupling is preserved at the level of individual chromosomes in cancer has been inaccessible to conventional epigenomic assays, which average signals across cell populations and cannot resolve single-chromosome heterogeneity. Here, we use antibody-functionalized atomic force spectroscopy to simultaneously map 5mC and H3K9me3 at the centromeres of individual metaphase chromosomes from non-tumorigenic, luminal, and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell models. Co-localized 5mC/H3K9me3 sites are mechanically stiffer than sites carrying either mark alone across the panel, revealing a cooperative biophysical signature of epigenetic crosstalk. Luminal chromosomes acquire the highest mark density, co-localization, and stiffness, whereas TNBC chromosomes show reduced density and diminished, though not absent, co-localization and stiffness, converging toward the low baseline of non-tumorigenic epithelium. TGF-β1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition reproduces this attenuated phenotype in luminal cells, linking it directly to a process central to TNBC aggressiveness. These biophysical parameters classify cancer versus non-tumorigenic chromosomes with near-perfect, cross-validated accuracy, and further resolve the two TNBC subtypes using colocalization-derived features alone (macro-F1 = 0.933 ± 0.026). These results establish the mechanical consequence of epigenetic mark co-localization as a single-chromosome-resolvable signature of centromeric organization, attenuated in aggressive breast cancer, and demonstrate a force-spectroscopy platform for mechano-epigenetic profiling of cancer chromosomes. TOC
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15000735/v4: The viscoelastic response of phase-separated polymers systems may deviate from bulk values at the nanoscale. However, current measurement techniques lack the resolution to unmask local variations. We previously demonstrated the advantages of using a focused, pulsed infrared (IR) laser to photothermally heat a sample locally during nanomechanical measurements with an atomic force microscope (AFM), with heating controlled by varying the laser repetition rate. Herein, we demonstrate this IR heating coupled with nano-Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (nDMA). First, we measured the storage and loss modulus of a homogenous copolymer at varying IR repetition rates (i.e., at varying sample temperature), demonstrating a viscoelastic modulus response that is typical near the glass transition temperature. Further, we varied the IR laser repetition rate while modulating the AFM probe between 5 Hz and 100 Hz. With time-temperature superposition, modulus master curves were constructed through the Williams-Landel-Ferry relation, and the shift factors of IR heating-coupled nDMA curves were used to estimate the relation between IR repetition rate and surface temperatures. Lastly, this technique was applied to a phase-separated polymer blend to demonstrate the utility of the technique to decouple the viscoelastic behavior of different phases by leveraging the high spatial resolution of AFM.
doi:10.1016/j.seppur.2026.140407: Membrane fouling remains a major barrier to the efficiency, durability, and practical deployment of membrane-based water treatment technologies. Although surface modification is widely used to mitigate fouling, the nanoscale interaction mechanisms governing foulant attachment and detachment remain insufficiently understood, limiting the rational design of antifouling membranes for specific foulant types. Here, silica particles, bovine serum albumin (BSA), and humic acid (HA) were selected as representative inorganic, proteinaceous, and natural organic foulants to systematically probe their interactions with pristine polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), polydopamine (PDA)-coated PVDF, and poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (PSBMA)-modified PVDF membranes using atomic force microscopy (AFM) force measurements. Approach force profiles were analyzed using extended Derjaguin–Landau–Verwey–Overbeek (DLVO) modeling to identify the dominant interactions controlling foulant attachment, while adhesion energies extracted from retraction curves were used to evaluate foulant detachment and membrane cleanability. PDA coating enhanced resistance to silica attachment by increasing repulsive interactions, but promoted stronger adhesion of BSA and HA through additional hydrophobic, hydrogen-bonding, and π-related interactions, leading to more irreversible organic fouling. In contrast, the zwitterionic PSBMA surface simultaneously suppressed foulant attachment and adhesion through strong hydration repulsion and electrostatic double-layer repulsion, resulting in superior antifouling and self-cleaning performance against all tested foulants. The nanoscale force measurements showed strong agreement with filtration behavior, demonstrating that interaction analysis can serve as a semi-quantitative descriptor of fouling propensity and cleanability. This work establishes an interaction-guided framework for designing membrane surfaces tailored to target foulants in water treatment.
doi:10.35848/1882-0786/aeafac: Advanced scanning probe microscopy (SPM) measurements have traditionally required highly specialized skills, but the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning has begun to transform how SPM is operated. This review surveys AI methods applied to SPM, organized by technique rather than chronology: unsupervised learning for feature extraction, support vector machines for real-time classification, convolutional neural networks for image analysis, Bayesian optimization for experiment planning, reinforcement learning for atomic and molecular manipulation, and object detection for feature localization. The emerging use of large language models as natural-language interfaces for microscope operation is discussed as a distinct topic. For each method, the operating principles and representative SPM applications are presented. This method-centric organization enables direct comparison of AI approaches applied to similar SPM tasks and clarifies the complementary roles—perception, decision-making, control, and orchestration—that each technique plays in integrated autonomous SPM systems.
doi:10.1002/jemt.70186: This paper studied the interaction between HepG2 cancer cells and NK-92 immune cells, employing an atomic force microscope (AFM) as the primary tool. The research mainly focused on the use of AFM to explore the effect of immune cells on cancer cells and revealed the relationship between the killing effect of immune cells on cancer cells and the mechanical properties of cancer cells. A novel method for quantifying in situ adhesion between the NK-92 cells and HepG2 cells was proposed, which provided insight into the relationship between the mechanical properties and the time of co-culture. Furthermore, the morphological and mechanical changes of HepG2 cells were detected using AFM. As co-culture time increased, the findings revealed a trend toward incomplete cell morphology. Reductions were observed in the heights, adhesion, and elastic moduli of HepG2 cells, along with an increase in cell surface roughness. The surface of membrane pores was visualized, and based on the obtained cell height data, the measurements of the size and depth of cell membrane surface pores were conducted. In conclusion, this research unraveled the complex interplay between the killing effect of immune cells on cancer cells and the mechanical properties of cancer cells. It offered a valuable perspective for understanding the interaction between immune cells and cancer cells, potentially paving the way for future therapeutic interventions.
doi:10.1007/s12195-026-00945-7: Abstract Purpose In solid cancers, inflammation and viral infections, two main fibroblastic functions have been identified: myofibroblast-like fibroblasts and inflammatory fibroblasts. In the tumour microenvironment (TME), these cancer-associated fibroblast (CAFs) subtypes are known as myCAFs, which generate a stiffened fibrotic extracellular matrix (ECM), and iCAFs, which secrete inflammatory cytokines to locally modulate the immune response. Yet, whether iCAFs contribute to shaping the ECM biochemical and biophysical properties remains understudied, mainly because robust in vitro models to generate fibroblast subtypes are lacking. Methods Here, we established an in vitro cell culture system based on murine NIH3T3 fibroblasts and stimulation by TGFβ1 and IL1α, alone or in combination, to induce fibroblast subtypes. Gene expression analysis of well-documented myCAF ( Acta2 / Tagln ) and iCAF ( Ccl2 / Il6 / Lif ) markers was performed. We compared these in vitro subtypes to myCAFs and iCAFs from publicly available scRNAseq data of tumour tissues from cancer patients. ECM deposition and remodelling were assessed by collagen contraction, fluorescence microscopy and atomic force microscopy. Results TGFβ1 induced a myCAF-like phenotype, while a combination of TGFβ and IL1α induced an iCAF-like phenotype. We found that, similar to myCAFs, both tumour-associated and in vitro iCAFs express Acta2 / Tagln as well as genes encoding typical ECM proteins, which correlated in vitro with the ability to contract collagen. Finally, fluorescence microscopy and atomic force microscopy revealed that in vitro both subtypes generate thick, layered and stiff matrices with highly aligned ECM. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that, besides myCAFs, iCAFs may also contribute to a pathological ECM. Our study provides new insights into the contribution of IL1α- and TGFβ1-induced fibroblast subtypes to ECM deposition and remodelling and puts forward a well-defined in vitro model to activate different fibroblast functions for future in-depth mechanistic studies of fibroblast subtype-specific roles in cancer and other pathologies.
doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0351819: BACKGROUND: Dural defects, either from trauma, tumor resection, surgical approaches, genetics, or spontaneously represent a significant clinical challenge in neurosurgery. Given the established efficacy of riboflavin-sensitized ultraviolet-A (UVA) photo-crosslinking in ophthalmology, this study investigated its feasibility and dose-response characteristics as a novel strategy to biochemically augment the mechanical integrity and strength of ex-vivo bovine dura mater. METHODS: Forty bovine dura mater specimens were treated ex vivo using riboflavin concentrations of 2, 4, or 8 mM combined with UVA irradiation at 0.3 or 3 mW/cm2. PBS-treated specimens exposed to UVA served as controls. Atomic force microscopy nanoindentation was used to measure the local elastic modulus in matched regions before and after treatment, enabling paired assessment of treatment-induced mechanical changes while minimizing inter-sample variability. Post-treatment stiffness, fold-change from baseline, and riboflavin dose-response relationships were analyzed statistically. RESULTS: Baseline elastic moduli were equivalent across all groups (mean approximately 52 kPa, p = 0.92). While UVA alone caused a modest approximately 2- to 3-fold stiffness increase, riboflavin-UVA treatment produced a dramatic, concentration-dependent effect. The highest treatment (8 mM RF, 3 mW/cm2 UVA) increased the elastic modulus 150-fold, from approximately 53 kPa to approximately 8,000 kPa. Post-UV stiffness exhibited a strong linear relationship with riboflavin concentration (R2 = 0.994), indicating a precisely titratable crosslinking effect. All treatment conditions were statistically distinguishable (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Riboflavin-sensitized UVA crosslinking substantially increases the nanomechanical strength of ex vivo bovine dura mater in a controllable, dose-dependent manner. These findings establish a proof of concept for biochemical reinforcement of dural tissue that might be used clinically. As a next step evaluation using human dura, macroscopic biomechanical testing, penetration-depth analysis, and safety assessment is warranted.
doi:10.1007/s12551-026-01467-2: Adhesion is a fundamental biophysical property describing how biological systems establish, maintain, and remodel interactions with their surrounding environment. Force spectroscopy, based on Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM), has emerged as a powerful approach for investigating these nanoscale interactions under physiologically relevant conditions. While existing literature often presents AFM as a general tool for nanomechanics or cellular topography, this review addresses a critical gap by focusing specifically and systematically on biological adhesion as a multidimensional mechanochemical phenomenon. We emphasize that biological adhesion cannot be reduced to a single scalar pull-off force; instead, AFM force-distance curves encode complex biophysical signatures that integrate force magnitude, adhesion energy, interaction range, rupture dynamics, and mechanically mediated detachment processes. In this review, we synthesize the physical foundations of adhesion, including nonspecific physicochemical forces, molecular recognition, polymer dynamics, and mechanical coupling, and demonstrate how these mechanisms translate directly into AFM force curves for cells, tissues, biomaterials, microorganisms, pathogen-modified host cells, and viral particles. We place special emphasis on the contrast between non-functionalized probes, which provide global adhesive fingerprints, and functionalized probes, which enable selected molecular interactions to be probed with piconewton-level sensitivity. Finally, we discuss current limitations and future perspectives regarding experimental standardization, statistical robustness, automated force-curve classification, and multimodal integration. By establishing a unified framework connecting fundamental physical forces, force-curve shape analysis, and biological applications, this review fills an essential gap for researchers seeking to decipher adhesion mechanisms at biological interfaces and within complex living systems.
doi:10.1002/smll.75659: ABSTRACT We report a nanomechanical study of ca. 1 µm thick crystalline films of the molecular spin crossover (SCO) complex [Fe(HB(1,2,4‐triazol‐1‐yl) 3 ) 2 ] across its thermal spin transition. Using quasi‐static and dynamic (1–100 Hz) indentation techniques, a step‐wise decrease in the modulus, E (from 9 ± 1 to 4.0 ± 0.5 GPa) and hardness, H (from 320 ± 40 to 170 ± 20 MPa) is observed when going from the low‐spin (LS) to the high‐spin (HS) state, which can be attributed to the reduced mass density of the HS phase. The significantly higher H / E 2 ratio in the HS state indicates its better resistance to wear and plastic deformation. On the other hand, only a modest modulus relaxation and no clear loss peak are observed at the transition point (330 K), likely due to ensemble averaging effects in nano‐sized domains as well as due to the gradual nature of the SCO in the films. Complementary nanoscratch experiments further confirm the impact of SCO on mechanical compliance, revealing an abrupt increase in scratch depth in the HS state. This comprehensive mechanical analysis helps to understand the coupling between spin state and mechanical properties and to optimize SCO materials for technological applications.
doi:10.1021/acsaelm.6c01367: Abstract The development of multifunctional electronic skin (e-skin) requires materials that combine mechanical flexibility with responsiveness to multiple stimuli. In this work, a flexible polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS)/La0.7Sr0.3MnO3 (LSMO)/multiwall carbon nanotube (MWCNT) composite thin film was fabricated via solution casting, using LSMO powder synthesized by a solid-state reaction method. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirm the formation of single-phase rhombohedral LSMO and the successful incorporation of PDMS, LSMO, and MWCNT components. The composite exhibits a smooth and uniform surface morphology, along with significantly improved thermal stability, retaining 70% of its mass at elevated temperatures. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements showed semiconducting behavior with an ∼17% change in resistivity over a temperature variation of ∼100 °C, enabling temperature sensing functionality. Furthermore, the composite exhibited pronounced negative magnetoresistance of approximately 27% under an applied magnetic field, arising from spin-polarized transport in the LSMO phase. Mechanical characterization revealed a tensile strength of ∼0.49 MPa, stretchability of ∼26%, and ductile deformation behavior, while nanoDMA measurements indicated a dominant elastic response with low viscoelastic loss. The multifunctional sensing properties arise from the synergistic interaction between the conductive MWCNT network and the magnetically active LSMO within the flexible PDMS matrix. Overall, the composite demonstrates a unique combination of thermal stability, mechanical flexibility, and dual sensing capability, making it a promising material for next-generation e-skin applications.
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c16183: Abstract Electrochemical processes involve transient phenomena, including nucleation and growth, phase transformations, dissolution, ion transport, and interfacial restructuring, which are difficult to capture simultaneously at nanoscale and in real time under electrochemical controls. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), originally developed for dynamic biological imaging, combines nanometer-scale spatial resolution with frame times of approximately 0.1–5 s/frame, extending into the subsecond regime, enabling direct visualization of electrochemical interfaces under operando conditions. This perspective highlights emerging applications of HS-AFM in electrochemistry, including electrodeposition, nanoparticle dissolution, corrosion, lithiation-induced morphological evolution, protein adsorption, and nanobubble dynamics. HS-AFM reveals that mechanistic insight often resides in transient, nonequilibrium pathways rather than equilibrium structures alone. Advances will enable real-time nanoscale correlation of interfacial structure, kinetics, and electrochemical function.
doi:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117900: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) enables mass sensing through resonance-frequency changes of microcantilevers, but quantitative measurements can be affected by calibration and environmental factors. Here, we investigated whether a calibrated AFM cantilever and controlled mass loading could provide nanogram-scale mass estimation. Cantilevers were cleaned and calibrated by force-distance measurements, and resonance acquisition parameters were optimized under ambient conditions. UV-curable resin droplets were locally deposited on the cantilever to generate mass loading, and resonance-frequency shifts were measured and analyzed using a mass-spring model and finite-element simulations. Increasing resin mass produced progressive decreases in resonance frequency, demonstrating a consistent relationship between mass loading and cantilever resonance behavior. Finite-element simulations reproduced the resonance responses and supported the mass estimates obtained from the experimental measurements. These findings establish a calibration and modeling framework for resonance-based mass quantification using conventional AFM cantilevers and provide a basis for extending quantitative mass analysis to microstructures and biological assemblies.
doi:10.1038/s43246-026-01370-z: Flexoelectricity offers a universal route to electromechanical coupling in centrosymmetric materials, but its macroscopic output is often constrained by the weak strain gradients attainable in planar thin films. Here, we introduce a femtosecond-laser strategy to sculpt hollow nanoblister arrays in anatase TiO2 thin films, creating high-curvature architectures that amplify flexoelectric response. The blister morphology can be continuously tuned from isolated domes to line-shaped structures through laser-parameter control. Cross-sectional analysis reveals that nanoblister formation arises from localized TiO2/Pt interfacial delamination followed by shell buckling. Piezoresponse force microscopy confirms enhanced local polarization within the hollow blisters and their mechanical and electrical tunability. By coupling nanoscale blister curvature with macroscopic substrate bending, the device achieves multiscale strain-gradient amplification, delivering an output voltage of 0.516 V and a 21.5-fold enhancement over planar TiO2 films. Finite-element simulations corroborate the geometry-driven mechanism, establishing hollow-structure engineering as a general strategy for high-performance flexible flexoelectric devices. This study uses a femtosecond-laser to sculpt hollow nanoblister arrays in TiO2 thin films, creating high-curvature architectures that amplify flexoelectric response. By coupling this with macroscopic substrate bending, devices achieve an output voltage of 0.516 V and a 21.5-fold enhancement over planar TiO2 films.
doi:10.1016/j.ultsonch.2026.108101: Piezoelectric ceramics are being explored as mechanically powered materials for energy-environmental processes, but the relationship between energy transduction and material durability remains unclear. We examined four piezoelectric materials (BaTiO 3 , ZnO, K 0.5 Na 0.5 NbO 3 , and PbZr 0.53 Ti 0.47 O 3 ) under 40 kHz ultrasonic cavitation. The pressure criterion for reactive oxygen species (ROS) formation through water compression (2.8–8.1 GPa) exceeded the 1.13 GPa compressed-bubble pressure obtained from the bubble-collapse calculation. The electron-energy analysis provides a thermal-equilibrium reference rather than a prediction of plasma-derived ROS yields. The powder-free control showed only 0.7% and 1.9% tetracycline (TC) removal after 120 and 480 min, respectively. The open-circuit piezoelectric potentials calculated for 1 μm particles at the 1.13 GPa compressed-bubble pressure (9–210 V) exceeded the electrochemical thresholds (0.33–2.8 V), and the powders showed persistent contact-potential shifts up to − 318 mV and charge storage 32–55 times beyond the electrical double-layer limit. Cavitation-induced irreversible lattice strain and selective A-site ion leaching were accompanied by elbow-shaped TC degradation kinetics with performance declining from approximately 67% to 1–3% over five cycles. Mott–Schottky and impedance analyses indicated that interfacial electrochemical states were irreversibly altered. The tested powders are described here as finite mechano-electrochemical transducers whose operation is accompanied by irreversible material changes and declining activity. The relevant design criterion for sustainable piezoelectric environmental applications should include redox output, material lifetime, recoverability, and ion-release risk as well as the first-cycle activity.
doi:10.1002/adom.71936: ABSTRACT Long‐term stable photocarriers in van der Waals ferroelectrics can be controlled without external electrical or thermal stimuli, providing a platform for versatile photonic functionalities. A comprehensive understanding and spatial controllability of photocarrier relaxation dynamics under nanoscale structural variation are required for the three‐dimensional vertical stacking of photonic circuits. Nevertheless, structurally correlated observation of interlayer relaxation dynamics and its device‐scale realization have been limited by the spatial resolution of conventional near‐field optics and by irreversible domain‐switching methods. Here, an extendable flexoelectric platform is presented, in which an axial nanogap structure is combined with time‐resolved optical‐pump/electrical‐probe microscopy. The platform, which operates through van der Waals flexoelectric domain reconstruction, enables tunable interlayer photocarrier relaxation and switchable polarizability of interlayer electron‐hole pairs during interlayer tunneling. With respect to the spatial domain distribution, the asymmetric nanosecond‐scale interlayer dynamics are resolved through the decay profile of interlayer electron‐hole pair generation, the tunneling current, and spatial fluorescence‐lifetime mapping. The extendable flexoelectric platform provides a geometric route toward versatile optical functionalities in condensed matter physics.
doi:10.3390/mi17101129: The measurement of photothermal expansion via the deflection of a cantilevered probe has attracted attention as a tool for the investigation of condensed-phase materials. In the present work, I provide a simple theoretical analysis of signal generation by this micromechanical detection mechanism using the classical description of constrained thermal expansion. I relate signal intensity to the thermomechanical properties of the sample and the probe, and their contact geometry for the case of gradual excitation. The results support the general applicability of this configuration for the measurement of photothermal expansion and provide guidelines for optimization of the signal. I also provide a conceptual framework to analyze the measurement by describing it as a thermodynamic engine cycle, comprising a series of quasi-static processes. The engine is intrinsically inefficient when assessed in its capacity to convert energy into work, and the energy derived from light absorption is dispersed into the environment as heat. However, the thermodynamic efficiency is not a critical performance parameter when considering the main purpose of this mechanism, which is analytical.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78049-z: Polar vortices in ferroelectric heterostructures hold promise for high-density, energy-efficient nanoelectronics, but their controlled motion remains elusive due to strong pinning and lattice-coupled dynamics. Here, we report real-time observation of vortex boundary motion in PbTiO₃/SrTiO₃ heterostructures using localized trailing electric fields applied via a conductive atomic force microscopy (AFM) tip. The vortex boundaries show reversible motion that depends on both field polarity and AFM tip trajectory. By precisely steering the tip along specific paths, we achieve controlled, reconfigurable vortex boundary motion with remarkable stability over extended periods. In-situ scanning transmission electron microscopy further confirmed the controlled motion of the vortex boundary. Phase-field simulations reveal that this motion is governed by switching of the zigzag pattern at the vortex core, pinpointing the underlying physical mechanism. These results establish the feasibility of externally controlled vortex boundary motion, advancing both fundamental understanding of polar topological dynamics and prospects for next-generation polar-vortex-based nanoelectronic devices. The authors demonstrate reversible electric-field control of polar vortex boundaries in PbTiO₃/SrTiO₃ heterostructures, revealing their real-time motion and providing a pathway toward reconfigurable, low-power, high density topological nanoelectronics.
doi:10.1002/advs.77926: Cell state, growth, and mechanics are tightly connected properties underpinned by fundamental biological processes. Yet methods to quantify them simultaneously under physiologically relevant conditions, at resolutions sufficient to follow (sub)cellular processes, are still lacking. In particular, the correlation between cell state, mass, and mechanical properties during dynamic processes such as growth, differentiation, development, and disease remains poorly understood. Here, we develop experimental and theoretical approaches based on photothermally actuated microcantilevers integrated with optical microscopy to simultaneously monitor the morphology, mass, and quality (Q)-factor of single mammalian cells and larger cellular systems under culture conditions, with millisecond time resolution. We find that the Q-factor, a measure of mechanical energy dissipation, mirrors the mechanical properties of the cell, with the cytoplasm dominating as the largest and softest compartment. Our method reveals how cellular mechanical properties correlate with mass and depend on cell type, state, and growth. Applied to human spheroids, it further monitors how larger cellular systems regulate mechanical properties during development. Together, these measurements quantify mechanobiological parameters that have so far remained inaccessible, opening the way to a more complete characterization of how cellular systems regulate mechanics during fundamental processes of life.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aee5269: Materials with exceptionally low thermal conductivity are desirable for thermal insulation and waste heat recovery. While foams and aerogels boast ultralow thermal conductivities akin to air, lack of mechanical stiffness in these soft materials necessitates a paradigm shift in materials design that can offer thermal insulation and mechanical rigidity simultaneously. Here, we show that spun-cast layered hybrid organic-inorganic perovskite thin films, azobenzene ethyl ammonium lead iodides, exhibit a record-low thermal conductivity, down to ∼0.04 watts per meter per kelvin at room temperature, while maintaining mechanical rigidity with an elastic modulus of 7.7 gigapascals that surpasses that of most plastics, foams, and aerogels. This unusual combination of ultralow thermal conductivity and high mechanical rigidity is attributed to the specially engineered organic cations in the layered structure. Our finding highlights the potential of molecular engineering in hybrid layered structures to push the extreme of thermal insulation in dense, rigid solids.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2609.22567: The ratio of a structure's first two natural frequencies depends on its boundary conditions but not on its size, material density, or absolute stiffness, which multiply every frequency equally and cancel in the quotient. We use this to identify the boundary conditions of a small-scale beam or plate from two ratio measurements, without knowing its exact dimensions or material. The paper first establishes how the ratio $r=ω_2/ω_1$, and the fractional shift $Δr$ it undergoes when a boundary condition changes, respond to the two effects that matter at small scale: transverse shear deformation, through Timoshenko beam and Mindlin plate theory, and small-scale elasticity, through Eringen's nonlocal Timoshenko model. Using a locking-free Rayleigh-Ritz beam solver and a finite-element Mindlin plate solver, each checked against benchmarks, we find an asymmetry. The absolute ratio moves appreciably with thickness, by 12 to 14 per cent over the shear-deformable range, and with orthotropy, by 6 to 9 per cent, but only weakly with nonlocality; the shift $Δr$, by contrast, varies by less than 0.2 per cent over the full nonlocal range and by a few per cent under thickness change. Because $Δr$ is largely independent of these details, a measured shift identifies which boundary-condition transition a deliberate change of support has produced, with a resolution we quantify and verify against molecular-dynamics data. Two spring continua then extend the method to estimating support compliance, with the non-uniqueness of the tip-support case stated explicitly. The method needs no value of the small-scale parameter or the material constants.
doi:10.1002/anbr.70158: Hydrogel coatings provide a promising pathway to tailor and improve cell culture surfaces, maintaining bulk material properties desired for handling and optical measurement while providing cell–surface interactions vital for optimising cell behaviour. For immobilised hydrogels to be useful, layers of this structure must be robustly adhered to the substrate and able to withstand strain from sources such as tensile forces exerted by adherent cell lines and fluid streams in microfluidic devices. Plasma‐activated coatings (PAC) are investigated here as a method for robust and translatable hydrogel immobilisation. Results show that embedded radicals within the PAC can immobilise methacrylated poly‐vinyl alcohol hydrogels, forming nanometer‐thick (reagent‐free) to millimeter‐thick (photoinitiator‐assisted) hydrogel layers. Utilisation of the nanometer reagent‐free layer as a ‘primer layer’ before forming photoinitiator‐assisted millimeter‐thick layers is a novel approach that results in superior adhesion of the thicker gel layers. When used as a cell culture surface for MCF‐7 cells, E cadherin and vinculin signalling significantly ( p < 0.05) increased (for physiologically relevant High MA hydrogel compared to the glass control). This work therefore outlines the novel reagent‐free primer layer approach as a method for creating hydrogels with superior adhesion for in vitro culture of cells.
doi:10.1007/s10811-026-04012-6: Abstract Nitrogen deprivation is commonly applied to enhance lipid accumulation in microalgae for third-generation biofuel production. However, its influence on cell wall morphology and nanomechanical properties, which critically affect downstream processing, remains poorly explored. To address this gap, this study investigated the impact of nitrogen deprivation on these properties of the freshwater microalga Parachlorella kessleri using a multi-microscopy approach. Starvation did not lead to any significant morphological changes in either cell size (diameter and height) or cell wall thickness, but it significantly impacted nanomechanical properties: the Young’s modulus decreased by approximately 60% (from 1320.7 ± 415.1 to 535.8 ± 346.5 kPa), while surface roughness remained comparable between conditions (1.3 ± 0.5 and 1.9 ± 1.4 nm). Regardless of these similar roughness values, starved cells showed a strong negative correlation between roughness and stiffness, suggesting underlying structural changes not captured by morphology alone. Although biomass freezing for storage and subsequent thawing for analysis may have influenced absolute mechanical values, the comparative trends observed indicate that nitrogen deprivation preconditions the structural and nanomechanical features of this microalga. Therefore, this work highlights the potential of nanomechanical descriptors as complementary indicators for evaluating biomass processability in biofuel and bioproduct applications, opening the door to the development of more efficient and subsequently cost-effective cell disruption strategies.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-10778520/v1: Abstract Force–distance curves (FCs) are direct probes of tip–sample interactions in atomic force microscopy, but their dynamic content is often suppressed by filtering, averaging and quasi-static analysis. Indeed, in the forty years since the invention of the AFM, this hidden dynamic signal has been largely ignored, with exceptions restricted to the large oscillations associated with relatively large adhesive separations (snap from contact) or to time-averaged approaches that carry their own challenges. Using high-bandwidth interferometric detection, we directly measure fast FCs, including short-lived cantilever oscillations during snap-in, contact and pull-off. Two excitation mechanisms coexist: thermal fluctuations and transients generated by rapid changes in the tip–sample boundary condition. Cycle-resolved frequency and amplitude estimators provide time-local observables of the evolving cantilever–sample system within single FCs, creating a pixel-by-pixel mechanical-contrast channel that requires no external broadband excitation, resonant tracking or multi-pass imaging. A state-dependent harmonic-oscillator model incorporating van der Waals attraction, hysteretic capillary-bridge formation and rupture, hydration-mediated damping and repulsive contact stiffness partitions each FC into five interaction regimes and reproduces the observed responses. In repulsive contact, frequency shifts yield stiffness maps consistent with contact-mechanics estimates, enabling high-throughput stiffness mapping and localization of transient tip–sample events from individual pixels. More broadly, this hitherto hidden signal may pave the way for new ways of studying and exploiting Brownian motion in a variety of systems, providing the capability to follow time-resolved (non-)Markovian and (non-)ergodic dynamics mediated by the tip–sample interaction, including single-event dynamics.
doi:10.1016/j.envc.2026.101650: ABSTRACT Growing production and consumer use of plastics have contributed to the widespread occurrence of microplastics (MPs) in the environment – the upper size limit of MP is taken commonly as 5.0 mm. Photooxidation (PO) driven by ultraviolet (UV) radiation plays an important role in the transformation of MPs. This review summarizes the mechanisms of photooxidation under both direct UV exposure and indirect pathways and synthesizes findings from a wide range of environmental studies. Photooxidation begins when light absorption generates radicals that initiate chain reactions. Subsequent oxidation and chain scission introduce oxygen-containing functional groups, which alter crystallinity and weaken the polymer. The rate and outcome of this process depend on both the plastic formulation and its surrounding environment. Water may suppress surface oxidation by reducing UV penetration and oxygen availability, while also promoting physical fragmentation by penetrating oxidation-induced voids and facilitating crack propagation. Research evidence and field-derived carbonyl-index data for polyethylene and polypropylene indicate location-dependent aging across urban areas, agricultural soils, beaches and estuaries, and offshore surface waters. Urban and agricultural samples generally show lower median values, whereas stronger signals occur for beach polyethylene and offshore polypropylene. These patterns are descriptive rather than quantitative because the available studies are not methodologically harmonized and the environmental histories of sampled particles are largely unknown. The relationship between oxidation state and particle size distribution remains complex and is not resolved quantitatively. Based on this synthesis, future research should emphasize improved characterization of photooxidized MPs and standardized methodologies to better understand their environmental fate and implications across different compartments.
doi:10.1002/smll.75372: ABSTRACT Ongoing advances in scanning probe microscopy techniques are continually expanding the possibilities for nanoscale characterization and correlated studies of functional materials. Here, we demonstrate how a recent extension of piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM), known as interferometric vector PFM, can be utilized for simultaneously mapping the local crystallographic orientation and the domain structure of distributed grains in uniaxial ferroelectric polycrystals, without requiring complementary characterization techniques, such as electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD). By shifting the laser beam position on the cantilever, direction‐dependent piezoresponse signals are acquired analogous to classical vector PFM, but without the need to rotate the sample. Using polycrystalline as a model system, we demonstrate that the reconstructed piezoresponse vectors correlate one‐to‐one with the crystallographic orientations of the micrometer‐sized grains, carrying grain‐orientation and domain‐related information. We establish a versatile approach for rapid, multimodal characterization of polycrystalline uniaxial ferroelectrics, enabling automated, high‐throughput reconstruction of polarization and grain orientations with nanoscale precision.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2609.04015: Rapid advances in agentic artificial intelligence enable scientific systems to interpret open-ended objectives, combine heterogeneous information, invoke specialized tools, and revise experimental strategies as evidence accumulates. However, physical experimentation also contains many tasks for which agentic reasoning provides little advantage and can reduce reliability. Quantitative analysis, optimization, spatial targeting, validation, and instrument execution are often better posed as deterministic or algorithmic operations with explicit objectives and verifiable outputs. Here, we introduce a hierarchical architecture for autonomous experimentation that separates these roles. Agentic components interpret scientific intent, construct task-dependent experimental representations, evaluate accumulated evidence, and select high-level actions, whereas deterministic algorithms perform numerical analysis, coordinate selection, validation, and physical execution. We implement this architecture in piezoresponse force microscopy. Starting from a broad scientific question concerning the relation between local domain structure and polarization switching, the system constructs spatial descriptors from multichannel imaging, selects and analyzes local hysteresis measurements, adapts the spectroscopy waveform, and terminates the experiment when additional measurements cease to provide new evidence. The autonomous trajectory also identifies a confounding relationship between polarization state and domain-wall proximity and recognizes that the requested contrast is not independently represented within the available field of view. These results demonstrate a route toward scientific autonomy in which agents determine what evidence is required while algorithms determine how that evidence is acquired reproducibly and within validated physical constraints.
doi:10.1002/adfm.78114: ABSTRACT Programmable spatial control of excitonic quasiparticles is essential for realizing integrated photonic and information‐encoding platforms based on van der Waals heterostructures. A common strategy is electrostatic gating, which switches ferroelectric polarization and modulates excitonic responses through carrier doping and field effects. However, electrically driven polarization control requires additional electrodes and repeated voltage cycling, which may introduce charge trapping, polarization fatigue, and long‐term reliability constraints, complicating device integration and scalability. Here, we demonstrate flexoelectrically assisted exciton patterning by integrating MoSe 2 /CuInP 2 S 6 heterostructures onto periodic Au stripe arrays. Atomic force microscopy and Piezoresponse force microscopy reveal a periodic ferroelectric‐domain texture that closely follows the imposed surface Au stripe arrays corrugation. Meanwhile, a reduced‐order curvature‐based calculation analysis captures the periodic through‐thickness bending‐strain gradient and the associated flexoelectric polarization preference. The resulting ferroelectric landscape creates a domain‐dependent electrostatic environment in the adjacent MoSe 2 , producing a spatial redistribution of neutral exciton and trion emission together with modulation of their valley‐polarized response. By linking microscale deformation, flexoelectrically assisted ferroelectric‐domain patterning, and local excitonic behavior, this work establishes a scalable, fabrication‐defined route toward artificial excitonic lattices and spatially encoded optoelectronic architectures.
doi:10.1002/adfm.78109: ABSTRACT Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide is one of the most promising materials for non‐volatile memory applications due to its stability at small size scales and compatibility with robust fabrication techniques. However, the manufacture of phase‐pure ferroelectric hafnia remains an elusive challenge due to its sensitivity to synthesis and integration factors. This work reports on the use of argon plasma atomic layer annealing during atomic layer deposition growth as a route to enhance formation of the ferroelectric phase in hafnium zirconium oxide thin films. The introduction and the lengthening of the duration of atomic layer annealing enhance the ferroelectric properties of the films that form after a rapid thermal anneal. This is observed through Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and corroborated via scanning transmission electron microscopy, polarization measurements, and piezoresponse force microscopy. Qualitative analysis of the extended X‐ray absorption fine structure region reveals a change in the second‐nearest‐neighbor environment of the absorbing species in the amorphous deposit as atomic layer annealing duration varies. This change in the local structure creates a more favorable environment for ferroelectric phase crystallization, positioning atomic layer annealing as a processing route to facilitate hafnia‐based films with increased ferroelectric phase concentrations and virtually no polarization wake‐up.
doi:10.1016/j.newton.2026.100669: A central challenge in soft and biological physics is to relate microscopic structural rearrangements to the macroscopic mechanical response. In growing cell walls, which are biopolymer composites, irreversible deformation arises from the coupled action of elastic energy storage, viscous dissipation, and finite viscoelastic relaxation times. Here, we present a physics-based inversion framework that converts contact-resonance atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurements of living Arabidopsis epidermal tissues into nanoscale maps of stiffness, viscosity, and relaxation time across hypocotyl, pavement, and guard cell walls. The maps reveal strong spatial heterogeneity, with hypocotyl walls exhibiting higher moduli and viscosity than pavement and guard cells. Osmotic plasmolysis reduced elastic and viscous moduli by about 2-fold, indicating a major role for prestress. In contrast, the relaxation time remained nearly constant across wall types and conditions ( τ ≈ 2.6–3.1 μs ), consistent with a common nanoscale polymer relaxation process for all walls. This approach links experimentally accessible observables to local mechanical timescales in living active matter.
doi:10.59400/sv4502: The attenuation of vibration is one of the most important requirements in the manufacture of mechanical systems which are required to meet high speed, high load, light weight and precision control requirements. A traditional approach to vibration control is to redesign the structure, use passive damping or isolation systems, or use active control; the dynamic properties of the surface and interfaces are considered secondary. The aim of the present review is to adopt a surface-centered point of view by discussing how surface engineering can be used to achieve vibration attenuation by regulating the stiffness in contact, stabilizing the friction, damping at the interface, suppressing wear and enhancing the integrity of the surface. Functional coatings, solid lubricant films, viscoelastic layers, surface texturing, micro/nanopatterning, mechanical surface treatments, architectures for additive manufacturing (AM), and smart adaptive surfaces are critically discussed with regard to their vibration-control mechanisms and limitations. The focus is on tribo-dynamic coupling, i.e., coupling between friction, wear, lubrication and vibration, which can either dampen or amplify the dynamic response, depending on the feedback mechanisms between the components. The review also examines experimental characterization, multi-scale modelling, and applications in bearings, gears, machine tools, rotating machinery, automotive systems, aerospace components, robotics and biomedical devices. An integration of tribology, material science, manufacturing and structural dynamics is emphasized for effective vibration attenuation at surfaces. Standardized testing, predictive modeling, durability assessment, and system-level design frameworks are key to future progress. The surfaces of engineered systems should therefore be considered as more than just a physical barrier, but as a functional dynamic interface that can act as a quieter, more efficient, and more reliable mechanical system.
doi:10.1002/lpor.71834: ABSTRACT Phase separation and structural damage induced by ion migration represent primary bottleneck in blue perovskite light‐emitting diodes (PeLEDs). Herein, we developed heterocyclic diammonium cations, namely 3/4‐aminopiperidine (3AP 2+ /4AP 2+ ) dihydrochloride, for rigid perovskites, that effectively mitigates the degradation pathway. Compared to conventional phenylethylammonium (PEA + ), these piperidinium‐based dications promote the formation of a compact and mechanically reinforced perovskite film. This structural enhancement is quantitatively demonstrated through a remarkable increase in Young's modulus, with values reaching 24.5/20.1 GPa for 3AP/4AP‐incorporated films, representing 1.7/1.4‐fold improvements over PEA‐based counterparts, respectively. The observed improvement in mechanical properties is further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations. The strengthened framework substantially suppresses ion migration and preserves structural integrity, leading to exceptional spectral stability under both optical and electrical excitation. Consequently, we demonstrate high‐performance sky‐blue (488 nm) and pure‐blue (475 nm) PeLEDs with peak external quantum efficiencies (EQEs) of 18.8% and 9.8%, respectively. This work establishes molecular rigidification as an effective approach for developing high‐performance and operationally stable blue perovskite optoelectronics.
doi:10.64898/2026.08.04.742574: Abstract Phenol-soluble modulin α1 (PSMα1) is a cytolytic peptide secreted by Staphylococcus aureus that contributes to host-cell damage and biofilm stability, yet the relationship between its assembly behavior and function remains incompletely understood.
