Here, we combine cellular assays, molecular spectroscopy, and high-resolution structural approaches to elucidate how environmental conditions govern PSMα1 activity and supramolecular organization. Live-cell imaging and cytotoxicity assays show that PSMα1 accumulates at the plasma membrane of human cells prior to membrane permeabilization, linking membrane association to cytotoxic outcomes. This process is strongly attenuated by epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG). Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reveals two polymorphic canonical amyloid fibril architectures that share a conserved hydrophobic core and protofilament interface. In parallel, we identify pH as a key determinant of PSMα1 assembly pathways, driving a bifurcation between cross-β amyloid fibrils at extreme acidic and alkaline conditions and heterogeneous, long-lived, thermally stable α-helical nanotubular assemblies at acidic, near-neutral, and slightly alkaline conditions, which act as transient intermediates under highly acidic conditions. Together, these findings demonstrate that PSMα1 is not a single amyloid structure but a condition-dependent structural system in which environmental cues dictate assembly, membrane interaction, and cytotoxic function. This work provides a framework for understanding how polymorphic assembly of bacterial virulence peptides interfaces with host-cell interactions and suggests new avenues for targeting PSM-mediated pathogenicity. Statement of significance Staphylococcus aureus causes severe infections and uses the peptide PSMα1 to damage host cells and strengthen protective biofilms. Like many disease-associated proteins, PSMα1 self-assembles into amyloid fibrils, though their role in virulence remains unclear. We show that PSMα1 does not adopt a single architecture. Instead, environmental changes, such as those at infection sites, drive the peptide into distinct assemblies, including cross-β amyloid fibrils and unexpectedly stable nanotubes with α-helical features. Live-cell imaging shows PSMα1 accumulates at the plasma membrane before cell death, and that epigallocatechin gallate reduces membrane association and toxicity. These findings show that bacterial virulence can be regulated through…
doi:10.4103/mgr.medgasres-d-25-00145: Hypoxia is closely associated with tumor progression, metastasis, therapeutic resistance, and diagnostic challenges. The timely detection of hypoxia in live cancer cells is critical for early cancer diagnosis and for monitoring the effectiveness of anticancer therapies. Recently, there has been growing interest in non-covalent supramolecular design strategies for the development of hypoxia-sensitive sensors and prodrugs. Unlike the widely employed covalent approach, supramolecular chemistry eliminates the need for complex and time-consuming synthetic processes. Instead, the individual components of the sensor autonomously self-assemble into the desired structure. This review provides an overview of hypoxia-targeted and hypoxia-activated supramolecular probes, along with their mechanisms of action in tumor diagnosis and therapy. The supramolecular systems considered are classified according to the use of certain classes of macrocycles. The role of macrocyclic derivatives in the various proposed approaches and the response patterns of hypoxic targets will also be analyzed. Various representatives of the macrocyclic platforms, namely cyclodextrins, cucurbiturils, pillararenes, (thia)calixarenes, due to their properties such as molecular recognition, are used as molecular containers-carriers for pharmaceuticals and bio-organic fluorescent dyes. As a result of complex formation, the photostability and the signal-to-noise ratio of dyes increase. In addition, the solubility of hydrophobic guests in water improves, cytotoxicity is reduced, and targeted delivery promotes the accumulation of drugs/dyes in tumor cells.
doi:10.66021/pakmcr1837: Background: Multiple drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella Typhi is a public health threat. Due to their unique physicochemical properties, the manganese doped with zinc oxide nanoparticles (Mn-ZnO NPs) have become of interest as possible antimicrobial agents. Background: Multi drug resistant (MDR) Salmonella Objective: This research aims at synthesis and characterization of Mn-ZnO NPs and its antibacterial activity and hemocompatibility. Methodology: Chemical co-precipitation method was used for the synthesis of Mn-ZnO NPs. UV–Vis, XRD, EDX, SEM and FTIR were employed to characterize the nanoparticles. Red blood cell (RBC) hemolysis assay was used to evaluate hemocompatibility of red blood cell (RBC). The antibacterial activity against the MDR S. Typhi was determined by agar well diffusion method and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was determined by broth based assay. Results: The absorption peak of Mn-ZnO NPs is 372 nm and the pure ZnO NPs is 360 nm in the UV-Vis spectroscopy. XRD patterns display the hexagonal wurtzite structure and EDX analysis revealed the presence of zinc (56.3%), oxygen (38.2%) and manganese (5.5%). A few agglomeration and 40-80 nm particles were identified by the SEM. FTIR spectra showed typical peaks at 3412, 1635 and 435 cm-1. Hemolysis was 4.5% at 50 µg/mL and increased to 10.1% at 100 µg/mL. The diameter of the inhibition zone grew from 8.4 mm at 20 µg/mL to 16.8 mm at 60 µg/mL concentrations. The MIC of the MDR S. Typhi was 62.5 µg/mL. Conclusion: The concentration-dependent antibacterial activity of the Mn-ZnO NPs against MDR S. Typhi was observed and the relatively low hemolytic activity of the NPs was observed at low concentration. They need further investigation for their antimicrobial activity, action mechanism and for their safety concerning potential biomedical applications.
doi:10.13386/j.issn1002-0306.2025100189: To investigate the structure and stability of structured lipids enriched with conjugated linoleic acid (CLA-SLs), gas chromatography was used to determine the fatty acid composition and triacylglycerol configuration; additionally, high-performance liquid chromatography was used to determine the glyceride composition. Nanoscale hyperspectral imaging and Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy were employed to identify changes in oil particle morphology and functional group absorption peaks. Differential scanning calorimetry and oxidation induction time measurements were integrated to evaluate thermal behavior and oxidative stability, while concurrently monitoring changes in the acid value (AV) and peroxide value (POV) during storage. The results demonstrated that CLA was successfully incorporated into the glycerol backbone of high-oleic peanut oil (HOPO), yielding an overall content of 61.60% and a Sn-2 positional content of 49.78%. The glyceride composition was dominated by triacylglycerols (60.10%), among which 1-conjugated linoleic acid-2-oleic acid-3-palmitic acid triacylglycerol was the most prevalent (42.30%), indicating fatty acid molecular rearrangement during interesterification. The CLA-SLs particles exhibited a rod-like morphology. FT-IR spectroscopy revealed a red shift of the C=O peak to 1740 cm−1 after interesterification, with characteristic absorption peaks at 980 cm−1 and 950 cm−1, accompanied by weakened -CH2 stacking vibrations. Compared to HOPO, CLA-SLs displayed a lower melting point, enhanced meltability, and improved resistance to crystallization. The oxidation induction time of CLA-SLs was significantly longer than that of physically mixed CLA (P<0.05) yet remained shorter than that of HOPO. During storage, the AV and POV of the CLA-SLs were lower than those of free CLA and physically mixed oil, suggesting that interesterification partially delayed the oxidation rate of the system. These findings provide a theoretical reference for the precise preparation of target-structured lipids with improved stability.
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c04327: Abstract Time-resolved electroluminescence has been a central methodology for the development of LED devices. However, it still lacks quantitative theoretical descriptions of time-resolved electroluminescence. By combining the equivalent circuit models of semiconductor devices and the carrier dynamics of electroluminescence processes, here we have developed a voltage–current-emission framework to illustrate time-resolved electroluminescence from the pulse voltage as input, to injection current, and finally generate electroluminescence as output. The features of different LED devices can be quantitatively interpreted, confirming their universal applicability across LEDs with different materials and device structures. Importantly, the curves of time-resolved electroluminescence can be simulated to quantitatively describe the dynamics of current and carriers of the LED operation. In all, the voltage–current–emission framework offers theoretical guidance for achieving advanced LED devices for artificial intelligence (AI) technology.
doi:10.1002/anie.6330931: ABSTRACT Precise spatiotemporal control over chemical reactivity in living systems remains a formidable challenge, especially within deep tissues where light‐based methods suffer from limited penetration. Here, we present a γ‐radiation‐mediated catalytic decaging (γ‐RCD) strategy that harnesses hydrated electrons generated during low‐dose γ‐radiation to activate palladium catalysts, thereby initiating a catalytic cycle for the efficient release of functional molecules. Unlike conventional radiation‐triggered decaging, which relies on primary radiolytic species and suffers from inherently low yields, γ‐RCD achieves catalytic amplification, significantly enhancing radiochemical efficiency with G ‐values up to 25.8‐surpassing existing radiation chemistries by at least 20‐fold. We demonstrate the versatility of γ‐RCD in remotely activating fluorophores, as well as prodrugs with minimal radiation input. The selective activation of caged bioactive compounds in tumor‐bearing mice leads to potent antitumor effects and the translational potential of the γ‐RCD strategy. By integrating catalytic amplification with clinically relevant γ‐radiation, γ‐RCD opens a new avenue for precision medicine, functional biomaterials, and radiation‐responsive therapeutics.
doi:10.1038/s41529-026-00909-2: Abstract Spinodal decomposition can degrade corrosion resistance and embrittle materials. The ability to quickly, non-destructively detect spinodal decomposition via elastic property measurements before catastrophic materials degradation would represent a significant advance in materials testing. We demonstrate that spinodal decomposition can be detected in a binary Fe-Cr alloy via modulus stiffening using ex situ (and in situ) transient grating spectroscopy (TGS). The modulus stiffening is attributable to the convex dependence of the $$C{\prime}$$ C ′ elastic modulus on chromium content within certain compositional limits, which has been established by prior density functional theory studies. Over this range of initial chromium compositions, chromium partitioning due to spinodal decomposition raises the average $$C{\prime}$$ C ′ modulus such that the decomposed Fe-Cr alloy is stiffer than the initial solid solution. The presence and extent of spinodal decomposition in a 36 at. % chromium alloy are confirmed using atom probe tomography (APT), and are consistent with atomistic simulations that predict elastic modulus stiffening in the same alloy. The observed spinodal decomposition via APT is used to predict an expected modulus stiffening which, based on a simple model, agrees in sign and order of magnitude with the observed stiffening via TGS. The quantitative link between an observed composition change and a measured elastic response suggests TGS as a potential tool for non-destructive evaluation of spinodal decomposition in high-chromium ferritic phases in steels.
doi:10.1002/adma.75513: ABSTRACT Optical sensors are powerful tools to monitor biological systems. However, their practical deployment is often limited by environmental interferences such as autofluorescence, mechanical motion, and fluctuating illumination. These challenges are particularly pronounced in plants because they require and use light, which has impaired the use of (fluorescent) sensors for plant stress signals such as H 2 O 2 . Here, we present a ratiometric sensing platform that overcomes these limitations by integrating three spectrally distinct components: 1) an H 2 O 2 sensor based on aptamer modified near infrared (NIR) fluorescent single walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs, ∼1000 nm), 2) a stable NIR reference based on polyethyleneglycol modified Egyptian Blue nanosheets (EB–NS, 900–955 nm) and 3) a visible (VIS) signal (∼641 nm) to correct for the NIR autofluorescence tail of plants (>835 nm). This ratiometric approach enables robust signal correction under relevant perturbations, including leaf rotation and wind‐induced motion. Furthermore, it allows continuous H 2 O 2 monitoring under dynamically varying illumination conditions (>300%), resulting in a 75% enhancement in signal contrast compared to single‐channel detection. By spectrally resolving nanosensor signals and endogenous plant autofluorescence, this strategy enables in vivo monitoring of stress‐induced H 2 O 2 under realistic environmental conditions. It establishes interference‐resistant optical sensing and advances field‐deployable nanosensor technologies for precision agriculture.
doi:10.1021/acspolymersau.6c00190: Abstract Fracture in elastomers is commonly described by a critical energy release rate determined under uniaxial loading, yet its applicability to multiaxial deformation and microstructurally evolving materials remains unclear. Here, we quantify crack-growth onset in elastomer sheets under controlled biaxial stretching by combining energetic analysis with high-resolution measurements of near-tip deformation fields. For predominantly elastic elastomers, crack initiation occurs at a material-specific critical energy release rate that is insensitive to deformation biaxiality. In contrast, strain-induced crystallizing elastomers such as natural rubber exhibit a breakdown of this universality driven by a biaxiality-controlled transition in near-tip fields. Below a critical deformation state, crystallization remains spatially confined, with minimal impact on crack resistance. Above this threshold, crystallization expands across a larger region around the crack tip, significantly elevating the crack-opening displacement and the critical energy release rate. Consequently, fracture resistance is governed by the size and development of the crystallized zone rather than an intrinsic constant. These results delineate when elastomer fracture follows universal energetic laws versus deformation-activated structural transformations. This framework provides practical guidance for designing robust elastomers for complex loading in tires, soft robots, and biomedical devices.
doi:10.1021/acsnano.6c13264: Abstract As solid-state device architectures become increasingly complex, buried interfaces play a critical role in determining thin-film texture, morphology, and defect formation. However, resolving the structural features that control growth on nominally amorphous interlayers remains challenging because it requires three-dimensional sensitivity at high spatial resolution. Here, we combine four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy, fluctuation electron microscopy, and multislice electron ptychography to investigate ruthenium (Ru) thin films grown on an underlying amorphous Ta2O5 layer, a material stack relevant for next-generation electronic and spintronic devices. Although the Ta2O5 layer appears amorphous in conventional imaging, diffraction and depth-resolved ptychographic reconstructions reveal nanoscale β-Ta2O5-like ordered motifs near the Ru/Ta2O5 interface. These locally ordered motifs, together with the interfacial morphology, guide the orientation of the Ru layer and produce a textured, quasi-epitaxial film. The curved and atomically rough interface further induces depth-dependent strain gradients and promotes planar defect formation within the Ru layer. Collectively, these results demonstrate that hidden short-range order within nominally amorphous oxides can direct the growth of metallic thin films, providing a framework for engineering buried interfaces in advanced electronic and spintronic material stacks.
doi:10.1038/s41401-026-01960-0: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) represents the most prevalent form of malignant tumor and constitutes a principal cause of cancer-related mortality globally. Conventional therapeutic approaches predominantly induce apoptosis; however, their efficacy is often compromised by the development of drug resistance. Methuosis, a form of regulated cell death distinct from apoptosis, is characterized by aberrant macropinocytosis and the formation of cytoplasmic vacuoles. Aloperine (ALO), a naturally occurring antitumor alkaloid, has been observed to induce methuosis in cancer cells, although its precise molecular targets and mechanisms remain to be elucidated. This study investigated the anti-NSCLC effects of ALO using cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and mouse xenograft models. Through various assays, it was demonstrated that ALO directly interacts with VPS34 at the I760 residue and promotes TIP60-mediated lactylation of VPS34 at K356 and K781. This interaction inhibits VPS34 kinase activity and reduces intracellular PI(3)P production. The subsequent decrease in PI(3)P levels impedes Armus endosomal recruitment, disrupts Rab7 cycling, leads to the accumulation of macropinosomes, and impairs endolysosomal fusion, ultimately inducing methuosis. ALO exhibits significant antitumor efficacy and acts synergistically with cisplatin to co-activate methuosis and apoptosis, all while avoiding noticeable systemic toxicity. Collectively, ALO targets VPS34 lactylation and disrupts Armus/Rab7 signaling. When used in conjunction with cisplatin, it constitutes a safe and effective therapeutic strategy for NSCLC.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11400196/v1: Abstract Perovskite lasing diodes (PeLDs) require charge transport, optical gain, resonant feedback and high-density electrical injection to be integrated within a single thin-film device. Conventional hole transport materials (HTM) can, however, introduce non-radiative recombination and optical loss in nanophotonic cavities. Here we develop RS-3, a self-assembled monolayer that acts as a multifunctional hole-transport contact. The ultrathin RS-3 layer reduces buried-interface loss, increases net modal gain and preserves the periodic profile of the distributed-feedback (DFB) cavity after deposition of the quasi-two-dimensional N2F8 gain layer, enabling us to realize room-temperature current-assisted lasing under synchronized optical–electrical co-injection. RS-3-based light-emitting diodes also show lower turn-on voltage, higher current density and higher luminance than poly(9-vinylcarbazole)-based controls. Under pulsed optical pumping, the complete device lases near 550 nm at a threshold of 28 μJ cm⁻². With synchronized optical–electrical co-injection, the threshold decreases monotonically to 19 μJ cm⁻² as the pulsed current density increases to 1.30 kA cm⁻², with a minimum linewidth of 0.25 nm.
doi:10.1113/jp291096: Abstract Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster , zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans , frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active‐zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information‐processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits. image
doi:10.1007/s10971-026-07138-8: NiO octahedral nanoparticles with a face-centered cubic (fcc) structure were successfully synthesized via the sol–gel method, and the effects of annealing temperature and time on their structural, morphological, and antioxidant properties were systematically investigated. X-ray diffraction (XRD) results revealed that all samples crystallized in the fcc phase, except for the sample annealed at 300 °C. The lattice constant was calculated from XRD data, showing that increasing annealing temperature led to enhanced nanoparticle growth. Moreover, prolonging the annealing time initially resulted in a reduction of crystallite size, followed by stabilization at longer durations. Morphological and bonding characteristics were further confirmed by SEM and FTIR analyses. The antioxidant activity of the synthesized NiO nanoparticles was evaluated using the DPPH radical scavenging assay. Among all samples, the NiO nanoparticles annealed at 400 °C for 24 h exhibited the highest antioxidant activity (76.12 ± 3.43%), demonstrating that thermal treatment plays a critical role in controlling both the structural evolution and functional performance of NiO nanomaterials.
doi:10.5281/zenodo.23802272: Magnesium oxide (MgO) nanoparticles were successfully synthesized using a modified sol–gel combustion method with citric acid as a complexing agent. The structural, morphological, and physicochemical characteristics of the products were examined using FT-IR, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and dynamic light scattering (DLS). XRD patterns confirmed the formation of a cubic MgO phase, with crystallite sizes of 34–39.7 nm. SEM images revealed flake-like morphologies with particle sizes ranging between 43 and 48 nm, while AFM analysis showed surface roughness values consistent with ultrafine nanoscale features. DLS measurements indicated a monodisperse suspension with a PdI of 0.384. The antibacterial activity of the MgO nanoparticles was evaluated against Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli using agar well diffusion. The nanoparticles demonstrated noticeable antibacterial properties, producing inhibition zones of 4–5 mm, although lower than those produced by gentamicin. Interestingly, the inhibitory effect decreased with increasing nanoparticle concentration, suggesting a concentration-dependent interaction with bacterial cells. Overall, the study highlights the potential of MgO nanoparticles synthesized via sol-gel combustion as promising antimicrobial agents with tunable physicochemical features suitable for biomedical and environmental applications.
doi:10.1007/s10836-026-06265-y: Abstract Charge trapping and de-trapping phenomena are the core mechanism of Random Telegraph Noise (RTN), causing deviations in drain current amplitude over time due to the constant capture and emission processes of charges from the transistor’s channel. As the timing characteristics of oscillators, such as voltage-controlled oscillators and phase-locked loops, depend on the amplitude of the drain current, RTN impacts the stability of periodic signals by inducing variance in the length of the oscillation period (i.e., jitter). In this work, the time-domain jitter (under the concepts of absolute jitter, period jitter, and cycle-to-cycle jitter) induced by RTN in free-running and closed-loop oscillators is estimated. SPICE-level simulations demonstrate that the jitter of CMOS oscillators evolves differently depending on the arrangement of the oscillating structure and its timing behavior. The analysis is validated by straightforward analytical expressions and supported by experimental data from the literature. The relevance of this work lies in presenting a qualitative analysis of the RTN-induced jitter in CMOS oscillators for the characterization and evaluation of circuit design performance and reliability.
doi:10.1021/acsomega.6c09002: Abstract In this paper, we investigated the CNTs (single-walled carbon nanotubes)@SnO2@ZIF-67 material combined with a silicon micropillar structure, aiming to improve gas sensitivity for the NO2 sensor at room temperature and 46% relative humidity (RH). First, the gas composite materials of CNTs@SnO2 has been obtained by a hydrothermal process, then a gas sensor on a silicon planar substrate with good gas sensitive performance was fabricated by varying the doping ratio of the two materials. Second, ZIF-67 nanoparticle materials were doped in CNTs@SnO2 gas sensor to enhance the sensitivity of the sensor. Third, the good doping ratio of the CNTs@SnO2@ZIF-67 composite gas-sensitive material was then placed onto the silicon micropillar substrate, where the tiny structure increased the surface area and improved gas flow. It was found that the best results occurred when the micropillar’s diameter-to-depth ratio was 1:2, giving a 77 s response to 50 ppm NO2, a detection limit of 1.13 ppm, good selectivity, long-term steadiness, and dependable work at 46% RH. The results suggest a combined method that links material mixing with structural improvement, providing a new direction for making high-performance room-temperature NO2 sensors. Finally, the gas mechanism by the silicon micropillar sensor with CNTs@SnO2@ZIF-67 has been explored.
doi:10.1002/slct.74925: ABSTRACT Gallium (Ga)‐based nanorobotics and nanosystems (NR‐NS) have shown preclinical potential for precision oncology, offering strategies to address the limitations of conventional cancer therapies. Ga exhibits biologically relevant physicochemical and anticancer properties, including disruption of iron metabolism, inhibition of DNA synthesis, and induction of cell‐death pathways. However, the safety and therapeutic efficacy of Ga‐containing nanoplatforms depend on their chemical form, dose, formulation, biodistribution, and duration of exposure. Recent studies have investigated tumour targeting using functionalised nanosystems, externally controlled propulsion, and stimulus‐responsive drug‐release strategies, while artificial intelligence (AI)‐assisted navigation remains an emerging concept. Ga‐based platforms may also integrate therapeutic and diagnostic functions, supporting the development of theranostic applications and tumour monitoring. This review critically examines recent developments in Ga‐based nanorobotic and nanoscale systems for cancer therapy, molecular imaging, targeted drug delivery, and theranostics, with particular emphasis on studies published from 2021 onwards. Key mechanistic insights, nanofabrication strategies, targeting approaches, and emerging biomedical applications are discussed. Current challenges, including biocompatibility, immune interactions, manufacturing scalability, and clinical translation, are also highlighted. Overall, Ga‐based NR‐NS may offer promising opportunities for precision oncology, although their clinical applicability, therapeutic benefits, and long‐term safety require further investigation.
doi:10.1016/j.celrep.2026.118235: Genomic DNA is wrapped around core histones to form nucleosomes, which are organized in cells from euchromatin to heterochromatin with distinct genome functions. Although transcription is known to shape chromatin behavior in live cells, it remains unclear how different transcription systems act across chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments. We develop machine learning-assisted Repli-Histo labeling to classify euchromatin and heterochromatin classes (classes IA, IB, II, and III) and combine it with single-nucleosome imaging in living human cells. Nucleosome motion is progressively constrained from euchromatin to heterochromatin. RNA polymerase II inhibition by THZ1, DRB, or α-amanitin increases nucleosome motion in euchromatic classes IA and IB and in heterochromatin around nucleoli, but not at the nuclear periphery. In contrast, RNA polymerase I inhibition by CX-5461 selectively increases nucleosome motion in Class III heterochromatin around nucleoli. Our study reveals that Pol II and Pol I transcription shape chromatin behavior in distinct chromatin classes and nuclear subcompartments.
doi:10.1002/adem.71310: YbTa 3 O 9 with a perovskite structure exhibits an extremely low thermal conductivity and a thermal expansion coefficient comparable to that of yttria‐stabilized zirconia (YSZ), rendering it a promising candidate material for next‐generation advanced thermal barrier coatings. Nevertheless, systematic investigations on the mechanical properties of YbTa 3 O 9 remain insufficient to date. In this work, dense YbTa 3 O 9 bulks were successfully fabricated via pressureless sintering route. The flexural strength and flexural modulus of YbTa 3 O 9 were systematically characterized through three‐point bending tests combined with the digital image correlation (DIC) technique, while its fracture work and fracture toughness were measured using the single‐edge notched beam (SENB) method. The results demonstrate that YbTa 3 O 9 possesses superior strength and toughness. Specifically, its flexural strength and fracture work are significantly higher than those of conventional YSZ ceramics. Microstructural analysis of the fractured SENB cross‐sections reveals that the excellent mechanical strength and toughness of YbTa 3 O 9 are closely associated with its in situ formed nanodomain structure. The nanoscale domain structure induces crack deflection and crack branching behavior during fracture, which effectively enhances the strength and toughness of the material. This study provides a solid foundation for the engineering applications of perovskite‐structured ReTa 3 O 9 tantalates as high‐performance thermal barrier coating materials.
doi:10.1021/acsabm.6c01896: Clinical translation of 3D-bioprinted stem cell constructs requires standardized characterization across length scales and biological domains. This review critically evaluates imaging and analytical methods along the construct lifecycle: bioink rheology and printability, structural imaging by micro-computed tomography and optical coherence tomography, cellular analysis by confocal, light-sheet, and multiphoton microscopy, chemical mapping by vibrational spectroscopy and mass spectrometry imaging, and bulk and nanoscale mechanical testing. Beyond cataloging techniques, we propose a decision-oriented framework that maps critical quality attributes to workflow stages, distinguishes essential from optional measurements, defines a nondestructive-to-destructive testing sequence, delineates the operational limits of each method in opaque, thick, and cell-dense constructs, and separates established tools from emerging approaches such as machine learning-based quality prediction and digital twins. Finally, we outline the remaining needs for reference materials, standardized protocols, and recently updated regulatory pathways.
doi:10.1038/s44306-026-00166-8: α-MnTe is among the earliest discovered altermagnets with experimental evidence of A-type antiferromagnetic order above room temperature and spin-split bands. Here, we conduct a theoretical investigation of its magnetism based on the general symmetry-adaptive tensorial spin model, which not only confirms a Néel temperature of 340 K induced by the dominant 1st and 3rd nearest-neighbor Heisenberg exchanges, but also the hexagonal planar Néel vector polarization of the ground state due to both the single-ion and the two-ion anisotropies. The 6-fold rotation symmetry along z prohibits an in-plane easy axis when only considering rank-2 and rank-4 interactions, revealing the continuous ground state degeneracy. Subsequently, we show that the triple-resistance states can be realized by adopting MnTe as the barrier in the sandwiched magnetic tunnel junctions. By deliberately matching the Brillouin zone-resolved spin transport of both the barrier and the electrode, tunneling magnetoresistance up to ~5300% is obtained. Our work not only provides a fine database of the magnetism and transmission for MnTe, but also sheds light on the application in high-density spintronic memory devices.
doi:10.1007/s11696-026-05854-7: Abstract This study investigates the effects of 5% n-butanol and green-synthesized MgO nanoparticles on the engine performance, combustion, emission, and tribological characteristics of dual-biodiesel-based fuel blends. MgO nanoparticles were synthesized using guava leaf extract and characterized by SEM, TEM, FTIR, and XRD, confirming a flake-like morphology with particle sizes below 50 nm. The tested fuels included D100, A10PJ10D80, A10PJ10D75B5, and MgO-containing blends at 30, 60, and 90 ppm. Engine experiments were performed under different load conditions, while friction and wear behaviour were evaluated using a four-ball tribometer and SEM analysis. At full load, 5% n-butanol reduced BSFC from 0.328 to 0.322 kg/kWh and increased BTE from 30.4% to 30.5%, with concurrent reductions in CO, HC, and smoke opacity. Increasing MgO concentration further improved engine characteristics, with 90 ppm MgO achieving a BSFC of 0.305 kg/kWh and BTE of 32.4%, while CO, HC, and smoke opacity decreased to 0.0561%, 39.2 ppm, and 44.2 HSU, respectively. However, NO X increased from 910 to 975 ppm, indicating a trade-off associated with enhanced combustion intensity. Peak in-cylinder pressure and HRR increased to 70.9 bar and 39.4 J/deg, respectively. The optimum tribological response occurred at 60 ppm MgO, with COF and WSD decreasing to 0.0795 and 0.458 mm, corresponding to reductions of 14.97% and 18.94% relative to D100.
doi:10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c05105: Abstract The reactive carbosilane cationic surfactant (SK) has been studied for glass surface hydrophobization by blending with oligodimethylsiloxane derivatives, comprising epoxide (EO) and amine/alkoxyl motifs (AO), and deposition using three different approaches: spray, spin, and dip coating. Our contribution comprises the synthesis and structure characterization of a surfactant (1H NMR, FT-IR and Raman spectroscopies), the optimization studies for the layer deposition by tuning the chosen parameters and compositions, as well as the determination of contact angles and surface energies. The crucial roles of the layer composition and the deposition methodology were carefully investigated, especially in terms of the reactivity of SK with siloxane derivatives and glass surfaces. The experiments were supported by the calculation of solubility parameters (δ) and the dispersion (δD), polar (δP), and hydrogen bonding (δH, including its splitting into donor (δHD) and acceptor (δHA) counterparts) components utilizing HSPiP software, showing the possibility of appropriate component blending. The layer structure and morphology were studied via atomic force microscopy (AFM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analyses with Ar+ sputtering as well as in-depth Raman microscopy. It was demonstrated that spray coating was an inappropriate method since it provided an extremely rough layer, while dip coating provided a deposit of limited stability due to the presence of separated SK deposits. The optimal system comprised SK combined with AO by a spin-coating approach, enabling both surface hydrophobization and the formation of a stable, chemically attached layer on the glass surface.
doi:10.1002/adsu.70691: ABSTRACT The sluggish kinetics of oxygen electro‐catalysis, encompassing both oxygen evolution (OER) and reduction (ORR) reactions constitute a major bottleneck for energy conversion and storage devices like water electrolyzers and rechargeable metal‐air batteries. The spin state transitions from singlet ground‐state OH − /H 2 O reactants to triplet ground‐state O 2 products in OER (and vice versa in ORR) play a critical role in catalytic performance. This review presents an in‐depth exploration of spin state engineering of active sites in oxygen electro‐catalysts. We begin by elucidating the origin of spin states based on crystal field theory and the distinctions among low‐spin (LS), intermediate‐spin (IS) and high‐spin (HS) configurations. Subsequently, we discuss strategies for modulating spin states of active sites, supported by examples from oxygen electro‐catalysis. Advanced characterization techniques, including x‐ray absorption/Emission spectroscopy (XAS/XES), magnetic susceptibility measurements, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), Mössbauer spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT)/molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, are critically analyzed. Finally, we propose future research directions to advancing spin‐state‐related electrocatalysis.
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15011232/v1: Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell (PEMFC) catalyst layers have been probed experimentally and theoretically for decades. However, existing microscopy techniques lack the ability to perform quantitative analyses on the catalyst and ionomer distributions of catalyst layers. Since the microstructure of the catalyst layer has an influence on the electrochemical performance, the simulation of catalyst layer microstructures is of great importance. A physics-based simulation model was recently reported to predict the microstructure of the catalyst layer as a function of ink composition. We propose a workflow to characterize catalyst layers with the utilisation of Atomic Force Microscopy. The novelty of the workflow lies in the calculation of a statistical description of the catalyst layer (CL). This statistical metric is then used as a validation metric for a microstructural physics-based simulation model. The resulting simulation workflow can be used to predict the ink composition required to obtain catalyst layers with desired microstructural properties, paving the way towards more efficient PEMFCs.
doi:10.1002/mabi.70280: Biomedical polyurethanes (PUs) are widely investigated for blood-contacting devices, soft-tissue repair, tissue-engineering scaffolds, and smart implants owing to their tunable segmented structures, elasticity, and processability. However, aromatic PUs may generate potentially harmful degradation products, while conventional aliphatic PUs often suffer from insufficient hard-segment association, limited microphase separation, and inadequate long-term mechanical stability. Ordered hard-segment PUs, constructed from monodisperse, uniform-sized, or structurally well-defined hard segments, provide a molecular-level strategy to address these challenges by enabling cooperative hydrogen bonding and enhanced soft-hard segment microphase separation. This Review summarizes recent progress in their structural design, molecular construction, functional regulation, biomedical applications, and translational evaluation of ordered hard-segment PUs. Particular emphasis is placed on how hard-segment length, sequence regularity, symmetry, and content, together with soft-segment chemistry, surface/interface functionalization, blending or composite strategies, and network-based designs, regulate microstructure, mechanical performance, biocompatibility, and degradation behavior. The distinction between hard-segment ordering and hard-segment chemistry is further discussed, highlighting the importance of molecular regularity and packing capability rather than simply increasing hard-segment content. Finally, current challenges associated with biological validation, standardized evaluation, device-oriented design, and clinical translation are discussed, underscoring the need for structurally precise, interface-stable, application-specific ordered hard-segment PUs as advanced biomedical elastomers.
doi:10.1002/adma.75569: ABSTRACT Atomically thin amorphous carbon holds considerable promise for application in data storage, microelectronics, protective coatings, and flexible electronics. However, its device integration has been hindered by existing direct growth routes that rely on metal catalysts in contact with the substrate, causing metallic residue, film non‐uniformity, and the need for post‐growth processing. Here, we report the direct growth of monolayer amorphous carbon on a 2‐inch sapphire wafer via thermal chemical vapor deposition, in which a remotely positioned catalyst decomposes the carbon precursor into active carbon feedstock, keeping the growth substrate free of metallic contamination. X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy detects no catalyst residue across the wafer and confirms a highly sp 2 ‐hybridized carbon network, while electron microscopy reveals a random polygonal carbon network lacking long‐range periodicity. Raman and atomic force microscopy mapping confirm uniform and atomically smooth monolayer coverage, while electrical measurements establish its insulating character with ambipolar, gate‐tunable hopping transport. This synthesis approach provides precise control over thickness and uniformity at the wafer scale, enabling direct device integration of amorphous carbon for a wide range of applications, particularly as an interlayer for epitaxial growth of freestanding semiconductor membranes.
doi:10.1002/advs.78427: The Josephson junction (JJ) is the fundamental nonlinear building block of superconducting quantum technologies. Its macroscopic quantum tunneling physics underpins superconducting quantum computing, sensing, and communication, but scaling these platforms to utility-scale architectures places increasingly stringent demands on junction materials, interfaces, and fabrication. Practical quantum computing requires high reproducibility, low power consumption, tunability, a small device footprint, and resilience to noise and defects. This review surveys how advances in materials science, device characterization, and nanofabrication are addressing these challenges and redefining the figures of merit for next-generation JJs. This review also examines the evolution of fabrication strategies, from conventional multi-angle evaporation to foundry-compatible superconducting processes and the integration of emerging junction materials. Progress along these directions will determine how rapidly JJs move from laboratory-scale components to the foundation of industrial-scale quantum processors.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78977-w: Abstract Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. This task is ill-posed because multiple target-band signals can be compatible with a single source observation. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe 2 /h-BN/WSe 2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions.
doi:10.3389/feduc.2026.1955212: Background Digital twin (DT) technology is widely adopted in engineering practice but remains inconsistently defined and unevenly implemented in engineering education. Prior studies frequently conflate digital models, digital shadows, and bidirectionally synchronized digital twins, limiting conceptual clarity and cross-study comparability. As DTs expand into cyber-physical learning environments, clearer educational framing and evidence of learning impact are needed. Purpose This review characterizes how DT technologies are conceptualized, implemented, and evaluated in engineering education and identifies gaps in technical fidelity, pedagogical alignment, and assessment rigor. Scope/Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following PRISMA framework. Scholarly publications published between 2017 and 2025 were identified using structured database searches and screened using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The final corpus of 101 studies was analyzed for disciplinary context, DT taxonomy level, synchronization architecture, pedagogical function, and learning assessment approach. Results DT-related publications in engineering education increased sharply after 2021, with most implementations situated in manufacturing, mechanical, and civil engineering. Most studies employed partial or unidirectional DT architectures rather than fully synchronized twins. Instructional uses focused primarily on visualization, monitoring, and system exploration. Few studies employed validated instruments to measure learning outcomes, and most designs remained case-based or exploratory. Recurrent barriers included infrastructure constraints, limited faculty expertise, interoperability challenges, and ethical and governance concerns. Conclusions Current educational DT implementations exhibit rapid growth but substantial methodological heterogeneity. A unified DT classification framework that aligns technical fidelity with instructional intent is needed to support rigorous design, evaluation, and scaling of DT-enabled learning environments in engineering education.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78928-5: Abstract Dion–Jacobson two-dimensional hybrid organic–inorganic perovskites are promising ferroelectric materials, combining chemically tunable polarity enabled by their organic spacers with enhanced environmental stability. However, rational discovery remains difficult owing to uncertain phase formability and scarce, biased ferroelectric data. Here we show a staged, physically guided synthesis-by-design workflow that integrates learning from scarce ferroelectric data with structure-aware screening. Starting from 11 known ferroelectric compounds in this family, symbolic regression defines a descriptor-bounded ferroelectric-consistent region. Similarity-guided expansion and chemical filtering reduce 83,924 molecules to 1012 candidate divalent spacers, while machine-learned interatomic-potential relaxation and connectivity analysis identify 338 candidates retaining Dion–Jacobson connectivity. Sequential prioritization by connectivity retention, chemical similarity, energetic refinement and synthetic accessibility selects s −2-fluorobutane-1,4-diamine, leading to the synthesis of a PbI 4 -based Dion–Jacobson perovskite with experimentally confirmed ferroelectric switching. This prospective proof of concept shows how sparse property knowledge can be coupled with structural screening to prioritize organic spacer candidates for experimental synthesis.
doi:10.1002/chem.71849: The revelation of the crystallization mechanism of zeolites is the key to shifting their synthesis from trial-and-error methods to predictive approaches. This review introduces the traditional and recently emerging green synthesis methods of hierarchical zeolites and compares their crystallization mechanisms from the perspective of synthesis strategies. Then, by discussing the classical and nonclassical theories, it analyzes the crystallization mechanisms of different synthesis strategies for hierarchical zeolites and finds that the research on kinetic control methods not only conforms to the theme of green and environmentally friendly synthesis at present but also can further explore the mechanism of zeolite crystallization. Finally, this review also presents the research results of the emerging machine learning-assisted zeolite structure design, which will bring new possibilities for the future realization of hierarchical zeolite structure design and directed synthesis through predictive methods.
doi:10.1021/acs.macromol.6c01298: Abstract Long polymer chains are inevitably tangled in knots that compromise their mechanical strength, yet how knot complexity governs the molecular rupture mechanism remains poorly understood. Here, we study the mechanical failure of single polyethylene chains bearing knots of varying complexity (3–7 crossings) using reactive molecular dynamics simulations across multiple pulling rates. We identify a consistent three-stage failure mechanism comprising entropy-driven tightening, enthalpy-driven tightening, and bond rupture. The breaking force follows a stretched exponential decay with knot complexity, while the elastic modulus grows exponentially; topological confinement therefore plays two competing roles. Analysis of bond-breaking locations indicates a gradual crossover in the failure mechanism: knots with lower minimum crossing number (31, 41) break predominantly at the knot entrance/exit, whereas knots with higher minimum crossing number (71) rupture within the densely packed core. Bond angle analysis shows that the geometric distinction between entrance and core regions diminishes with increasing minimum crossing number, providing a structural rationale for the boundary-to-core shift and demonstrating that knot topology offers a tunable handle on both polymer strength and stiffness.
doi:10.1002/adom.71993: ABSTRACT Near‐infrared fluorescence recognition becomes challenging when coupled to micro‐action execution, because the task requires not only weak‐signal detection but also reliable compression of high‐dimensional optical information into low‐dimensional events constrained by real device physics. Here, we develop a cross‐layer architecture integrating a far‐red‐centered wavelength‐selective organic photodetector array, programmable current‐domain encoding, and a physics‐guided vision‐to‐motion interface. The DIBSQ: SBDTIC bulk‐heterojunction device exhibits a 590–765 nm response band, with a peak external quantum efficiency of 15.3% at 657 nm, a peak responsivity of 83.9 mA/W at 721 nm, rise/fall times of 19.63/18.11 µs, and a −3 dB bandwidth of 17.6 kHz. Pixel‐by‐pixel calibration and write‐then‐recheck measurements of the 6 × 6 array are used to quantify spatial dispersion and temporal fluctuations for a hardware uncertainty budget, yielding four recognition‐current states centered at 0, 10, 20, and 30 nA. A two‐level threshold and binary encoding scheme then converts the recognition result into two‐bit X/Y motion primitives. In an independent 1 µm piezoelectric closed‐loop experiment, the physics‐guided neural network achieves an RMSE of 7.1 nm.
doi:10.1201/9781003455141: This book covers the microsystem integration aspects of biosensors. It provides an in-depth examination of how biosensors function within complete diagnostic systems and delivers a thorough foundation in both the biological and engineering principles essential for developing functional biosensor platforms. Fundamentals of Biosensor Microsystems begins with the introduction of biomolecules as bioreceptors and their possible target detection. It follows by elaborating on the techniques of biomolecules extraction, surface modification and treatment, and immobilisation and functionalisation of biosensors. A wide range of biosensors are detailed in this book with deep fundamental explanations. It also explains the fundamentals of biosensor targets, receptors, target manipulations, biosensor detections, and data analyses. The authors also examine various types of sensors, including electrochemical biosensors, electrode-based biosensors, chemical biosensors, optical biosensors, mass-sensitive-based biosensors, micromechanical-based biosensors, microfluidic and dielectrophoresis biosensors, magnetic-based biosensors, and thermal biosensors. The authors also connect the reader with the applicable emerging technologies related to biosensor microsystems such as point-of-care via lab-on-chip, biosensors, and Internet of Things. This book is intended for senior undergraduates, postgraduate students, researchers, engineers, industry professionals, and medical practitioners who are involved in the field of biosensors and microsystems development.
doi:10.3389/fimmu.2026.1991810: Aberrant mechanical signals within the tumor microenvironment (TME)—including increased extracellular matrix stiffness, elevated solid stress, heightened interstitial fluid pressure, and fluid shear stress—have been established as key drivers of malignant tumor progression and metastasis. These physical cues are sensed by mechanoreceptors on the cell membrane (Piezo1, TRP channels, and integrin-FAK complexes), transmitted intracellularly through Rho GTPases and cytoskeletal dynamics, and ultimately reprogram transcriptional programs via nuclear translocation of transcriptional co-activators such as YAP/TAZ. Mechanical signals also drive metabolic reprogramming in tumor cells, particularly enhancing aerobic glycolysis (the Warburg effect), which results in massive lactate accumulation. Landmark discoveries in recent years have revealed that lactate serves as a substrate to drive histone and non-histone lactylation, directly coupling metabolic status with epigenetic regulation. Histone lactylation (e.g., H3K18la, H3K9la) activates pro-metastatic transcriptional programs by remodeling chromatin accessibility, promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), immune evasion, and therapeutic resistance; non-histone lactylation directly modifies cytoskeletal proteins (CFL1, vimentin, TPX2) and transcriptional regulators (Snail, YY1, PRMT1), enhancing the metastatic execution capacity of tumor cells at multiple levels, including cellular mechanical properties, migratory ability, and signal transduction. Importantly, mechanical signals, metabolic reprogramming, and lactylation constitute a mechano-metabolism-lactylation positive feedback loop, forming a self-reinforcing vicious cycle that continuously fuels tumor metastasis. This review systematically outlines the types and mechanotransduction mechanisms of TME mechanical signals, mechanically driven metabolic and transcriptional reprogramming, the multifaceted functions of lactylation in tumor metastasis, and the ultimate execution of the metastatic cascade driven by this positive feedback loop, and discusses potential therapeutic strategies targeting mechanosensitive pathways, metabolic vulnerabilities, and lactylation-modifying enzymes.
doi:10.64898/2026.10.25.761609: ABSTRACT The extracellular matrix of solid tumors exhibits spatially heterogeneous stiffness, yet how matrix stiffness shapes antitumor immunity in gastric cancer (GC) remains unclear. Here, we integrated anti-PD-1 clinical cohorts, GC specimens, single-cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses, a syngeneic mouse model, and tunable-stiffness hydrogels to clarify the immunological consequences of matrix stiffness. High matrix stiffness was associated with collagen accumulation and immune exclusion, while higher stiffness-associated transcriptional scores were related to poorer response to PD-1 blockade. Matrix softening markedly reshaped the immune microenvironment and enhanced the efficacy of PD-1 blockade. Mechanistically, stiff matrices promoted F-actin remodeling and YAP nuclear enrichment, driving LDHA-dependent glycolytic reprogramming in GC cells that further impaired the effector function of CD8⁺ T cells. Intriguingly, matrix softening was accompanied by enhanced IFN-γ-responsive PD-L1 expression in GC cells, consistent with adaptive immune resistance that may contribute to the limited antitumor effects of matrix softening alone. These findings suggest that matrix remodeling alleviates spatial and metabolic constraints on antitumor immunity, providing a preclinical rationale for combining matrix softening with PD-1 blockade in GC.
