doi:10.1021/acsmeasuresciau.6c00279: Abstract Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including those commonly described as exosomes, carry proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids that reflect the molecular state of their parent cells, making them attractive biomarkers for liquid biopsy-based cancer diagnosis. Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), which builds on conventional Raman spectroscopy (RS), can read this cargo as vibrational fingerprints, label-free or via targeted nanoprobes, with high sensitivity from small sample volumes. This review examines recent advances in SERS-based exosome/EV analysis for cancer diagnosis, following the workflow from sample to diagnostic decision. We discuss how EV isolation, characterization, heterogeneity, and coisolated lipoproteins and proteins shape the measured spectra and review plasmonic substrates, biosensor and microfluidic platforms, label-free versus label-based strategies, and Raman band assignments. Particular emphasis is placed on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) for decoding exosome/EV SERS fingerprints, from conventional classifiers to deep learning (DL) and explainable AI, together with common pitfalls such as small cohorts, spectrum-level data leakage, class imbalance, and a lack of external validation. Applications in cancer detection, classification, subtyping, and monitoring are summarized for prostate, lung, breast, and pancreatic cancers, and representative platforms are compared by analytical performance and clinical readiness and against circulating tumor DNA and circulating tumor cell assays. Finally, we offer perspectives on the standardization, reference materials, shared spectral databases, and multicenter validation needed for clinical translation, positioning AI/ML-assisted SERS as a complementary tool for cancer triage and monitoring.
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15011161/v1: Agentic AI, powered by large language models, has increasingly been applied within self-driving laboratories and here we review its emerging role in self-driving microscopy. Microscopy is an unusually demanding target as each experiment is a sequence of interdependent decisions about where to measure, at what resolution, through which modality, and often on ambiguous evidence. We review recent demonstrations across atomic force, scanning tunneling, and transmission electron microscopy and examine how agentic systems can lower the expertise barrier to advanced characterization, transfer strategies between platforms, mine laboratory records for reusable protocols, generate and screen hypotheses, and bring simulation into the experimental loop. We also highlight and examine the limitations that currently constrain these systems. Agents can lose track of the scientific goal as a session outgrows their context window. They also remain poor judges of their own competence, making failure particularly difficult to anticipate in open-ended research. Flexible reasoning must therefore sit on deterministic, physically constrained control, with safety limits enforced outside the model. Human oversight can be the safeguard, but a human acting only as an approval or rejection gate risks forfeiting what scientists contribute most — questioning how the problem was framed in the first place. Designing agentic systems that preserve that contribution and address the current limitations is, in our view, the defining challenge for the field.
doi:10.1002/adfm.79324: ABSTRACT Phototransistors offer intrinsic gate‐controlled gain amplification, providing much higher responsivity than photodiodes, but this advantage is generally limited by the gain‐speed trade‐off: high gain typically relies on long‐lived trapped carriers, which inevitably slows the photoresponse. Although low‐dimensional semiconductors and hybrid heterojunctions have improved responsivity and detectivity, they still predominantly operate through slow, trap‐mediated gain, leaving the trade‐off unresolved. Here, sub‐10 nm organic–inorganic single‐crystalline van der Waals heterojunctions are introduced to decouple gain from slow carrier trapping. Specifically, a bilayer molecular crystal (C 6 ‐DPA) is integrated onto a monolayer MoS 2 channel. Reducing the heterojunction thickness to the exciton diffusion limit, localized Frenkel excitons in C 6 ‐DPA efficiently undergo interfacial charge separation and transfer across the type‐II interface, while the separated charges rapidly modulate the MoS 2 channel conductance through the field effect. Gain therefore arises from efficient channel gating rather than prolonged trapped‐carrier circulation. The resulting phototransistors achieve a responsivity of 1.07 × 10 5 A W −1 , rise/decay times of 771.2/809.8 µs, and a specific detectivity of 2.19 × 10 15 Jones under their respective optimized operating conditions. These results demonstrate that the gain–speed trade‐off in phototransistors arises primarily from trap‐mediated gain mechanisms and can be mitigated through exciton‐engineered ultrathin single‐crystalline organic–inorganic van der Waals heterojunctions.
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2610.37581: Much of the water that matters most - flowing through biological cells and membranes, percolating through soils and rocks, or processed by filtration and desalination technologies - is not bulk water. It is water in nano- and molecular-scale confinement or at interfaces. Nanoscale water is therefore central to many challenges of our time, from the global water crisis and the water-energy nexus to catalysis, electrochemistry, and health. Beyond its applications, nanoscale water has emerged as a rich scientific field in its own right: discoveries are accumulating rapidly, revealing that confinement and interfacial forces produce a range of behaviours absent in the bulk. Sometimes this amounts to a renormalization of bulk properties; in other cases, new and non-intuitive phenomena emerge - exotic phases, anomalous transport, and dielectric responses that defy continuum expectations. A convergence of atomically precise nanofluidic devices, novel spectroscopies and microscopy approaches, and machine-learning-accelerated simulations is now exposing the molecular mechanisms behind these behaviours. This Perspective argues that the recent findings should not be viewed as isolated nanoscale anomalies, but as evidence for a molecular regime of water in which continuum descriptions must be rethought and molecular-level understanding becomes essential. Recognising and exploring this regime should have consequences ranging from fundamental physics to the rational design of future technologies that rely on water and dissolved ions.
doi:10.1002/adfm.79304: ABSTRACT Garnet‐type solid‐state electrolytes (SSEs) enable safe, high‐energy solid‐state lithium metal batteries (SSLMBs) but suffer from poor interfacial contact and lithium dendrite penetration. Here, we report a machine learning ‐guided interfacial strategy that constructs a self‐adaptive graded interphase from a B 105 M 40 composite interlayer (BiOCl: Mg 3 N 2 = 105:40). The interphase features a lithiophilic LiMg phase at the bottom to ensure intimate Li/LLZTO contact, a porous Li 3 Bi phase to accommodate lithium plating/stripping, and Li 3 N/Li 3 OCl phases that enable fast ionic transport and dendrite suppression. The self‐adaptive gradient interphase maintains stable contact with lithium metal during cycling. As a result, B 105 M 40 ‐Li||LLZTO||B 105 M 40 ‐Li symmetric cells exhibit a high critical current density of 15 mA cm −2 and stable cycling over 5000 h at 14 mA cm −2 . Full cells retain 93.7% capacity after 1000 cycles with LiFePO 4 cathodes at 2.0 C, while those paired with high‐voltage LiNbO 3 @LiNi 0.8 Co 0.1 Mn 0.1 O 2 cathodes exhibit cycling for over 1000 cycles at 1.0 C. Moreover, the strategy is applicable to sulfide SSEs, offering a universal interfacial design for long‐life SSLMBs.
doi:10.1088/2634-4386/aeb971: Abstract Short-term plasticity (STP) is fundamental to temporal information processing in biological neural systems but remains difficult to realize efficiently in neuromorphic hardware, where conventional implementations often require additional circuit elements or digital control, resulting in increased complexity and overhead. Memristive electrochemical random access memory (ECRAM) devices naturally exhibit non-equilibrium ionic dynamics that produce transient conductance modulation; however, these behaviors are typically treated as undesirable variability or tolerated as side effects in memory-centric computing paradigms. In this work, we instead exploit these volatile dynamics as a computational primitive for implementing STP through a cross-layer device–circuit–system co-design framework. We introduce a delay-feedback leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron architecture co-designed with ECRAM synapses that exploits activity-dependent conductance modulation with negligible additional circuit overhead. The architecture integrates ECRAM-based synapses with a tunable delay-feedback spike-generation path, enabling transient device dynamics to directly modulate neuron excitability and synaptic efficacy. We used experimentally characterized ECRAM devices exhibiting transient conductance modulation (∼1.5 kΩ per spike) to develop a compact behavioral model suitable for circuit-level simulation. Circuit simulations demonstrate two key STP behaviors – synaptic facilitation and intrinsic excitability modulation – while consuming 2 pJ per spike, and the same device-driven mechanisms extend across multiple neuron topologies. Network-level analysis further demonstrates frequency-selective spike processing, allowing individual synapses to act as tunable temporal filters within spiking neural networks. These results demonstrate that non-equilibrium ECRAM dynamics can be transformed from a device non-ideality into a native hardware substrate for STP and energy-efficient temporal computation in neuromorphic circuits.
doi:10.1007/s44337-026-00735-0: Parasitic and viral pathogens impose a significant global health burden. Early, accurate, and affordable diagnostics remain scarce, as do therapeutics that provide a sterile cure. To address these burdens, aptamers have been proposed as potential alternatives. They offer enhanced stability through conformational modulation, cost-effectiveness, scalability, and long-term storage without loss of activity. Thus, they have been extensively explored in biomedicine for biomarker detection, imaging, diagnostics, and targeted therapy in the management of NTDs. Recent studies on aptamers against viral targets such as SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1, Hepatitis, Leishmania, Trypanosoma cruzi , and Plasmodium falciparum have shown improved affinities, detection limits, potent inhibitory effects, and enhanced therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models. Aptamer-based biosensors, fluorescence, magnetic separation, and paper-based LFAs require minimal reagents and equipment, enabling true field deployability. Nuclease susceptibility, rapid renal clearance, and challenges in scalable manufacturing are being addressed through chemical modifications and accelerated via Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (SELEX). This review evaluates current aptamer applications for viral and parasitic NTDs, outlines obstacles, and highlights pathways toward clinically viable, low-cost diagnostic and therapeutic platforms.
doi:10.3389/fbioe.2026.2011948: Polymeric membranes and thin films are integral components of a wide range of medical devices, where their mechanical behaviour directly influences device function, durability, and interaction with surrounding tissues. Their design is challenging because physiological environments impose complex combinations of cyclic loading, deformation, fluid pressure, shear, viscoelasticity, and interfacial stresses. In this narrative review, we discuss a biomechanics-guided approach to designing polymeric membranes and thin films that link physiological mechanical requirements to polymer chemistry, material architecture, fabrication processes, interfacial behaviour, and device-level performance. We first examine the mechanical characteristics of representative biological tissues and discuss how these properties can be translated into material design requirements. We then review major polymer classes and manufacturing strategies, with particular emphasis on how molecular structure, crosslinking, fibre alignment, porosity, and multilayer architecture influence mechanical behaviour. The review further considers mechanics-transport coupling, stimuli-responsive membranes, fatigue and degradation under physiological conditions, and application-specific challenges in cardiovascular, neural, dialysis, and wound-care devices. Finally, emerging approaches based on machine learning, 4D printing, organ-on-chip systems, and biomimetic ultrathin membranes are discussed. We highlight that effective biomechanics-guided design requires consideration of not only elastic stiffness, but also anisotropy, viscoelasticity, fatigue, interfacial mechanics, degradation, and physiological conditioning. This framework provides a basis for integrating material and mechanical design considerations into the development of multifunctional polymeric membranes for medical applications.
doi:10.1002/smtd.71149: Ag icosahedrons, characterized by the size-dependent distribution of strain fields, has garnered increasing interests across disciplines from crystallography to materials science. However, the metastability arising from such intrinsic strain greatly restricts the available synthetic routes. Here, we present a facile aqueous-phase electrodeposition technique for the robust synthesis of Ag icosahedrons. By decreasing the Ag reduction rate, we achieve enhanced control over the electrodeposition kinetics, as quantitatively evidenced by the apparent activation energy. The pronounced kinetic stability allows for the synthesis of particles up to 5 µm in size within 10 min (Pretreatment time: 48 h). Through systematic variation of applied potentials, currents, and electrolyte compositions, we enable the design of Ag icosahedrons with tunable hierarchical structures. These structured particles can be effectively employed as surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) substrates for pesticide detection. This work establishes a stable and pure model system that facilitates the straightforward synthesis of metastable structures.
doi:10.1186/s43074-026-00294-8: Abstract High power laser processing is a cornerstone of modern manufacturing and advanced scientific research, where parallelization is critical for increasing throughput and enabling new capabilities. However, simultaneously achieving high power handling, multi-beam parallelization, and compact optical integration remains a long standing challenge. This trade-off is addressed by establishing a wafer scale silicon carbide (SiC) meta-optic platform that combines three key elements: the thermomechanical robustness of SiC, an aperture matched architecture for dense multi-beam integration, and a scalable semiconductor compatible manufacturing process. The platform integrates a SiC diffractive optical element (DOE) with a wafer scale 26 element SiC metalens array. The array consists of metalenses with a diameter of 1.15 cm and a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.5 and exhibits high uniformity across the array, with a 3σ focal length deviation of 10.73 μm, corresponding to 0.11% of the designed focal length, and an average image normalized focusing efficiency of 93.90%. This architecture converts a large aperture input beam into multiple focusing channels compatible with millimeter to centimeter scale industrial laser beams, with 4, 9, and 26 beam configurations fabricated and characterized. As the front end component exposed to the full incident beam before power division, the SiC DOE experiences the most stringent power handling condition in the architecture and exhibits a continuous wave laser induced damage threshold of 6.11 kW/cm 2 , confirming its suitability for high power beam splitting. These results establish a SiC meta-optic platform for robust high power multi-beam photonic systems and suggest a scalable route toward next generation parallel laser processing.
doi:10.1088/1361-6463/aeaef7: Abstract Purgeless atomic layer etching (ALE) of SiO 2 has been proposed to simplify the conventional ALE process by eliminating the purge steps, and its feasibility for achieving self-limiting etching has been experimentally demonstrated. However, subsequent investigations revealed that the process suffers from non-ideal behaviors: ‘dragging decrease’ caused by residual fluorocarbon species, and ‘over-etching’ that may cause etch-per-cycle drift. These phenomena weaken the self-limiting nature essential for ALE yet have not been mechanistically studied in the purgeless ALE regime. In this study, simultaneous in situ ellipsometry and residual gas analysis are used to directly track residual gas-phase CF x species and examine their temporal relationship with dragging decrease and continuous over-etching in purgeless ALE. Oxygen is introduced into the etching step to scavenge residual species and suppress the instabilities, and the process monitoring confirms that O 2 addition effectively reduces residual CF x radicals, leading to the simultaneous suppression of dragging decrease and over-etching. According to the results, application of the oxygen-assisted approach in purgeless ALE successfully restores the self-limiting characteristics and ensures process stability. By mechanistically identifying the instabilities and demonstrating their suppression, this work supports the practical implementation of purgeless ALE.
doi:10.1002/cey2.70338: ABSTRACT Electrode homogeneity, specifically the uniform distribution of lithium ions and state of charge (SOC), is paramount to unlocking the full performance, safety, and longevity potential of lithium‐ion batteries. SOC heterogeneity triggers detrimental local phenomena such as particle fracture, lithium plating, and accelerated degradation, which become critical bottlenecks for next‐generation high‐energy and fast‐charging batteries. Although formidable, this challenge can be addressed through advanced characterization that links microscopic dynamics to macroscopic design. This Perspective highlights interferometric scattering microscopy (iSCAT) as a transformative, lab‐accessible optical technique capable of real‐time, nanoscale visualization of lithiation dynamics and phase transitions within individual electrode particles under operando conditions. We elucidate how iSCAT uniquely quantifies lithiation fronts, domain formation, and particle‐to‐particle variability, revealing the origins of heterogeneity rooted in crystallographic orientation, electrode architecture, and kinetic limitations. Crucially, these nanoscopic insights directly inform rational electrode design strategies, including functionally graded architectures and low‐tortuosity structures, to spatially homogenize electrochemical reactions. We conclude by outlining the integration of iSCAT with multi‐modal characterization and machine learning, projecting its pivotal role in accelerating the development of high‐performance, durable energy storage systems.
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c04262: Scaling resistive random-access memory (RRAM) toward ultradense crossbar arrays for high-density storage and neuromorphic computing requires precise nanoscale control of conductive filaments for reliable multilevel operation. Here we directly visualize and modulate nanoscale filament evolution in substoichiometric Y2O3-x thin films using high-resolution in situ conductive atomic force microscopy (c-AFM) with controlled current compliance. The switching threshold systematically increases with increasing oxygen stoichiometry, while filament evolution is continuously modulated by varying the applied bias. The initially formed larger filaments persist and dominate subsequent switching events during multicycle measurements. Using the c-AFM tip as a nanoscale mobile top electrode, single-point switching reveals localized switching with a lateral influence of approximately 20 nm, defining a crosstalk length scale. These results directly link oxygen stoichiometry, microstructure, filament evolution, and switching length scales, providing new insight into nanoscale filamentary switching and physical guidelines for scaling polycrystalline memristors toward ultradense memory and neuromorphic applications.
This study investigates the structural, lattice dynamic, electronic, and Fermi surface evolution of exfoliated few-layer 1T'-molybdenum ditelluride (1T'-MoTe2) under hydrostatic pressure. Using a combination of atomic force microscopy, in-situ high-pressure micro-Raman spectroscopy, temperature-dependent four-probe electrical transport, and high-field magnetotransport within a diamond anvil cell, the material's phase behavior was systematically traced up to extreme pressures. Atomic force microscopy confirms uniform, atomically smooth flakes with an average thickness of 8.5 nm (approximately 12 layers). High-pressure Raman spectroscopy demonstrates a universal blue-shift of optical phonon modes and identifies a structural crossover near 4.8 GPa, characterized by the complete quenching of the vibrational mode and a sharp reduction in mode pressure coefficients. Electrical transport measurements reveal a pressure-induced transition from a semiconducting state with a 42.1 meV thermal activation energy to a fully metallic state at 8.2 GPa, displaying Fermi-liquid quadratic resistance scaling at low temperatures under 14.5 GPa. Furthermore, high-field magnetotransport at 12.8 GPa unveils a large, non-saturating magnetoresistance reaching 420% at 9 T alongside distinct Shubnikov–de Haas quantum oscillations. Fast Fourier Transform analysis resolves fundamental oscillation frequencies at 142 T and 285 T, corresponding to a light cyclotron effective mass of 0.12 electron masses. These findings establish hydrostatic pressure as a powerful knob for tuning electronic band structures and Fermi surface topology in transition metal dichalcogenides, providing critical insights for the development of strain-engineered quantum devices and phase-change electronics.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-77789-2: Memristors are promising for neuromorphic computing electronics, yet scaling is hindered by the difficulty of fabricating ordered nanoscale electrodes. Here, we report an angstrom-scale graphene-edge memristor with a geometrically defined 0.34 × 0.34 nm2 crossed-electrode area. Key to this achievement is our stress-distribution-based technique that enables intact graphene transfer onto smooth vertical sidewalls without damage. Combining this technique with chemical mechanical polishing and wafer-level bonding, we demonstrated an angstrom scaled memristor based on a geometrically defined 0.34 × 0.34 nm2 crossed-graphene-edge electrode area, which exhibits a switching ratio exceeding 103 and volatile characteristics. The device also demonstrated significant low-power (370 nW) potential in the demonstration of the probabilistic bits system. Our work establishes a viable strategy for high-density memristor arrays and introduces a mechanical approach for manipulating 2D materials in unconventional geometries and integrating them into next-generation nanodevices. Here, the authors report a stress engineering method to fabricate graphene-edge memristors with a geometrically defined 0.34 × 0.34 nm2 crossed-electrode area, showing volatile characteristics and their application for low-power probabilistic computing.
doi:10.1088/2631-7990/aeabdc: Abstract Atomic-level manufacturing (ALM) represents a critical evolution in manufacturing technology, extending the progression from macro- and meso-manufacturing to micro- and nano-manufacturing. As an advanced capability, it has the potential to transform materials science, serve as a foundational “root technology” for new industrialization, and is emerging as a key arena of global competition among manufacturing leaders. This review systematically explores the concept of ALM and its transformative impact on future industries. It first analyzes the essence and significance of ALM, emphasizing how precise and scalable control of atoms can revolutionize production by enabling atomic-precision manufacturing, atomic-scale structural fabrication, and ultimately the on-demand placement or creation of individual atoms. This review then discusses implementation effects and potential demand, highlighting broad application prospects in integrated circuits, quantum information, aerospace, and precision instrumentation. It also reviews technical systems and development status, focusing on the core elements that underpin ALM, including simulation and design software with supporting databases, atomic-level processing, atomic-level assembly, and atomic-level characterization, and summarizes representative domestic and international achievements and the major technical challenges across these areas. By examining contemporary products, the paper demonstrates practical ALM-enabled advances in fields such as novel materials and high-end sensors, illustrating its role in driving future industrial upgrading. In addition, it clarifies the distinctions and connections between ALM, integrated-circuit manufacturing, nano-manufacturing, and quantum technologies, thereby outlining ALM’s unique characteristics and development trajectory. Finally, the review traces the historical origins of ALM and assesses future breakthroughs, forecasting wide-ranging impacts on industry, the economy, and society.
doi:10.1117/1.jmm.25.4.041805: BackgroundThe current carbon hard mask (CHM) film deposition techniques are not suited for mitigating x-field and x-wafer thickness and topography variation. This variability also affects both lithography patterning and post-etch critical dimension (CD) variability. Strategies to address this issue often include restrictive design rules, CHM polish, a more complex process flow. However, these solutions end up negatively impacting yield, cost, and process development cycle times. Canon’s work on nanoimprint lithography has led to the development of inkjet adaptive planarization (IAP). IAP provides planarization performance that is agnostic to feature size, aspect ratio, or pattern densityAimWe aim to collect data from wafers coated with IAP and other current available CHM-like techniques to characterize the impact of systematic local topography on the patterning process window.ApproachTopography data (AFM, Interferometry) as well as patterning data from wafers with IAP and CHM-like planarization is presented.ResultsAFM scans across 15% and 75% pattern density regions on the field demonstrated a 10× reduction in topography with IAP compared with other CHM-like planarization methods. Full-field interferometry data with ∼2.5 μm pixel size and noise levels of ∼5 nm show that IAP planarized wafers have x-field topography that is within ±5 nm. The patterning data that were collected were also consistent with an increase in the process window for the IAP planarized wafer.ConclusionsAs semiconductor manufacturing moves to more advanced nodes, CD variation plays an increasingly important role in determining whether performance and yield targets are achieved. Our data show that IAP can generate significantly flatter surfaces, which results in a wider process window, underlining the importance of controlling incoming wafer topography for critical layers.
doi:10.1038/s41598-026-69212-z: Abstract The trade-off between scanning speed and image quality constrains the application of terahertz near-field imaging in high-throughput scenarios. In this study, quantitative models were established to link the proportional (P) and integral (I) parameters to image quality—quantified by the Brisque score—at 0.4 Hz and 0.5 Hz using second-order polynomials (R 2 = 0.65 and 0.60). The optimal parameters were found to be frequency-dependent. At a scanning frequency of 0.4 Hz, the optimal proportional gain P and integral gain I were 560 and 575, respectively, yielding a minimum Brisque score of 35.70. At 0.5 Hz, the optimal values shifted to P = 100 and I = 225, with a corresponding minimum score of 41.11. With these optimized parameters at 0.5 Hz, the Brisque score decreased from 49.10 (obtained with conventional settings, P = 400, I = 300) to 41.11, representing a 16.3% relative improvement, while the scanning speed increased by 25%. This work offers a quantitative framework for PI parameter optimization in terahertz near-field imaging, enabling fast, high-quality imaging in biomedical and other applications. The frequency-dependent trends reported are based on experiments conducted at 0.4 Hz and 0.5 Hz, with supplementary validation at 0.3 Hz and 0.6 Hz.
doi:10.1093/nsr/nwag477: Abstract The rapid development of micro- and nanoscale devices has driven demand for wafer-scale, high-resolution nanostructure fabrication, which remains challenging for current nanolithography technologies. Here, we develop a cost-effective and high-throughput lithographic strategy for patterning sub-wavelength nanostructures over wafer-scale areas. This strategy is based on perfect conformal contact lithography combined with vacuum ultraviolet excimer irradiation at 172 nm. Using specially modified, transferable polymethyl methacrylate as a photoresist, the resulting approach enables high-fidelity, wafer-scale (8 inch) replication and fabrication of nanoscale (100 nm) patterns on both rigid and flexible substrates. We further develop a physical pattern-transfer method enabling high-resolution, solvent-free lift-off over large areas with 100% yield. The applicability of the lithography and pattern transfer strategy is demonstrated by the fabrication of 6560 nano-gap electrode structures over an area of 4 cm2 for MoS₂ transistor fabrication. Together with the demonstration of 12 representative transistors exhibiting on/off ratios approximately 108 and a large-aperture (10 cm) metalens enabling high-quality long-distance imaging, these results confirm the applicability of the proposed lithography and pattern transfer strategy across both electronic and optical devices.
t:c6c0221379dda44d: Excitons in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are highly sensitive to external stimuli, allowing control of resonance energies and lifetimes through electric and magnetic fields, heterostructures, moire potentials and mechanical strain. Observations of single-photon emission (SPE) near sample edges, wrinkles, and strained nanobubbles have motivated strain-engineering aimed at realizing localized emitters in 2D materials. The origin of these emitters remains unclear and prior studies have relied on far-field spectroscopy with strain profiles inferred separately through topography, limiting direct correlation between local strain and excitonic response. We directly probe strain-modified excitonic spectra in monolayer WSe$_2$ using cryogenic scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM). We compare two strain-engineering techniques, nano-indentation and patterned substrates, used to produce SPEs. At 9 K, we spatially resolve exciton resonance shifts with sub-diffraction limit resolution, simultaneously measuring near-field optical response and topography. We observe that strain transferred from nano-indentation into a deformable polymer substrate differs from that produced by draping TMDs over patterned dielectric pillars. Adhesion and tearing during plastic deformation drive a compressive exciton blueshift, while draping produces dominant tensile strain. Comparing the strain model results to the experimentally observed energy shifts shows that the nano-indentation strain is over an order of magnitude smaller than previously inferred, due to puncturing of the fragile monolayer, whereas pillar-strained devices remain intact under more modest strain. These differences suggest SPE arises from complex, strain-mediated interactions rather than simple confinement potentials, establishing s-SNOM as a powerful probe of quantum emission in strained 2D materials.
t:c8b4fba5a345e320: The interaction between plasmons and magnons is a long-sought phenomenon with implications for fundamental physics and spintronics applications. In three-dimensional systems, this coupling is suppressed by the large mismatch in energy scales, but two-dimensional (2D) plasmons with gapless dispersion can overlap with magnons over a broad spectral range. Despite numerous theoretical predictions, experimental observation of magnon-plasmon interaction has remained elusive. In this work, we study a first-of-its-kind hybrid plasmon-magnon platform based on 2D materials. By deploying scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) with terahertz radiation, we image propagating plasmon wavepackets at a graphene/NiPS$_3$ interface and track their dynamics across the antiferromagnetic transition of NiPS$_3$. We observe a clear renormalization of the plasmon-polariton dispersion concurrent with the onset of antiferromagnetic order. With complementary Raman scattering and nano-terahertz spectroscopy, we unveil spectral weight redistribution and dielectric screening changes, potentially associated with the multi-magnon continuum, as the underlying mechanism. These results provide solid evidence of coupling between plasmon and antiferromagnetic order, marking a cornerstone for a potential platform for hybrid magnon-plasmon interactions in 2D materials, opening avenues for coherent spin-plasmon devices and tunable terahertz spintronic components.
doi:10.1016/j.solmat.2026.114798: Three conjugated highly branched polymers incorporating variable amounts of functionalized propylenedioxythiophene (ProDOT), triphenylamine (TPA) and fluorene are proposed in the current work for use as dual functional electrode materials in energy storage smart window (ESSWs) devices. In a three-electrode setup, these polymers attained the highest areal specific capacitances of 1.77 mF·cm −2 at 10 mV·s −1 and 0.56 mF·cm −2 (69.42 F·g −1 ) at 0.02 mA. Two of the polymers, with a lower branching arrangement, showed a notably electrochromic (EC) efficiency of 567/606 cm 2 ·C −1 and extremely short coloration/bleaching times (0.22 s/0.55 s and 0.48/0.47 s). The polymer with the highest pseudocapacitive performance, which displayed an optimal macromolecular packaging and better electroactivity ensured by the balanced content of TPA and ProDOT units, was selected for use as electrode material in ESSW prototypes with a glass(PET)/ITO/polymer//gel electrolyte/PEDOT:PSS/ITO/glass(PET) configuration. Notably, the capacitances consistently increased up to 2.07 mF·cm −2 (43.93 F g −1 ) at a charging current of 0.01 mA with the contribution of PEDOT:PSS in the ESSW prototype, which delivered a power density of 1.47 μW·cm −2 (50000 W·kg −1 ) at 1 mA, and a Coulombic efficiency of 98.5 %, albeit 47 % capacitance decay after 500 cycles. This also exhibited a coloration efficiency of 435 cm 2 ·C −1 , fast coloration/bleaching times of 0.57/2.27 s, a luminous transmittance modulation of 35.73 %, and only 1 % relative decay of the transmittance variation at 395 nm after 500 cycles. These findings underscore the potential of HB polymers as dual-functional electrode materials in ESSWs, as well as the possibility of performance modulation through structural composition. • Highly branched polymers are investigated as dual functional electrode materials. • Thin coatings obtained therefrom show interconnected grains morphology. • In three electrode set-up, electrochromic efficiency of 567/606 cm 2 ·C −1 is obtained. • The electrochromic and capacitive functions are demonstrated in flexible/rigid devices. • Coloration efficiency of 435 cm 2 ·C −1 and power density of 1.47 μW·cm −2 are obtained.
doi:10.26434/chemrxiv.15011188/v2: Deep-blue phosphine-oxide hosts are compared by energy levels and photophysics, almost never by microstructure—yet order and film morphology are routinely read as proxies for how well a host will carry charge. Here three related hosts are compared from primary particles to film relief with documented, protocol-tested descriptors. The tert-butyl-substituted S3 host emerges as the least ordered on every scale: the lowest X-ray ordered fraction at every baseline setting, the shortest film correlation length at matched scan size, micrometre-scale relief and the lowest decomposition temperature, while only the S1 host shows lattice fringes. This structural disorder coexists with a smooth hole-only device response. The S3 hole-only device shows a single, nearly ideal relaxation with a capacitance close to the geometric value and an apparent hole mobility of about 5 × 10⁻⁷ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹, comparable to that of the far better-ordered S1 host, although a bias-independent relaxation time is also consistent with the RC response of the layer stack. Long-range disorder in these hosts is therefore compatible with a clean hole-only response, and microstructure alone is not a reliable screen for transport.
doi:10.1016/j.jwpe.2026.111170: Topographical membrane surface patterns are a promising approach for increasing transmembrane flux and reducing foulant deposition. In this study, we investigated the anti-biofouling propensity of TFC membranes with micrometer-scale patterns. Unlike most studies in literature, where biofouling of patterned membranes was investigated without feed spacers and in short-term tests, we considered a) spacer-filled channels and b) advanced biofouling stages. We thereby addressed an important knowledge gap regarding the interaction between membrane surface patterns, spacer geometry, and biofouling dynamics. We found no substantial differences between surface-patterned and reference flat membranes regarding anti-fouling propensity in biofilm growth and membrane cleaning. Differences were marginal to modest ( < 10 % ) for most and not significant for all assessment methods (feed channel pressure drop, active/total biomass in final biofilms, and camera image data). To explain these findings, we suggest that the anti-fouling effects of micrometer-scale membrane surface patterns may be a) overridden by millimeter-scale feed spacers that dominate flow characteristics and biofouling dynamics and b) ultimately hindered by biofilm coverage in advanced biofouling stages. Besides, image-based fouling monitoring of advanced biofouling stages was critically assessed. Although no substantial differences between flat and surface-patterned membranes were observed for the geometries (micrometer-scale line-and-groove patterns and millimeter-scale conventional spacers) and conditions (accelerated biofouling tests without permeation) tested, anti-fouling effects of patterned membranes in spacer-filled channels may occur under alternative operating conditions and geometry scales. We therefore recommend further biofouling tests, incorporating permeation, real desalination feed waters, adapted cleaning procedures, different pattern scales, and novel feed spacer geometries.
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh7105: The escalating crisis of antimicrobial resistance, particularly among Gram-negative bacteria, demands innovative therapeutic strategies. Here, we present a dual-targeting lipid nanoparticle-chimeric phage (AbLCP) system engineered to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria. Our design integrates a genetically modified M13 phage displaying anti-lipopolysaccharide (LPS) antibodies with polymyxin B conjugation, which is further encapsulated within anti-LPS antibody-functionalized lipid nanoparticles. This system overcomes the fundamental limitations of conventional phage therapy, enabling efficient cellular internalization, endosomal escape, and potent intracellular bactericidal activity. In murine models of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, AbLCP achieved superior bacterial clearance and up to 10 3 -fold reduction in bacterial burden at a 10 3 -fold lower effective dose than free polymyxin B, with 67-fold selective accumulation at infection sites, and attenuated systemic inflammation and preservation of gut microbiota. Mechanistically, AbLCP neutralized LPS to suppress inflammation and induced a lethal bacterial stress response. This work establishes a transformative nanophage platform that merges synthetic biology with nanomedicine, offering a promising strategy against MDR bacterial infections.
doi:10.34133/research.1459: The core dilemma of senescence mitigation lies in the disrupted and even detrimental communication between senescent cells and local immune cells. Existing delivery methods cannot precisely establish protective intercellular communication channels across cell types within the enclosed lesion cavity. In this study, we utilize Chinese microneedle technology for precise, minimally invasive localization of aged lesions, and to release spatially targeted and temporally sustained dual-field to create intercellular communication channels between macrophages and senescent cells. The unique physical properties of this Chinese microneedle system confine the current path to specific spatiotemporal windows, releasing an electro-field while simultaneously activating dynamic van der Waals forces that release functionalized hydrogel microparticles, thereby superimposing a vita-field. Within the dual-field active zone, the electro-field not only attenuates cellular senescence but also forms a communication channel from senescent cells to macrophages, driving macrophages into a hyperactivated state. Meanwhile, the vita-field stabilizes the macrophage membrane, enabling long-term, stable communication between hyperactivated macrophages and senescent cells. Ultimately, the intercellular communication channels established by this Chinese microneedle system alleviate cellular senescence and apoptosis, supporting the repair of aged lesions.
doi:10.1016/j.est.2026.123821: Triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures offer a compelling route for designing porous electrodes with tunable architectures for electrochemical applications such as redox flow batteries. In this study, we fabricated carbonaceous TPMS electrodes, including gyroid, diamond, IWP, and cubic geometries, using digital light processing, and evaluated their performance in single-electrolyte flow cells using an organic redox couple. The printing process and subsequent thermal treatment produced conductive porous electrodes that closely replicated the intended TPMS geometries, preserving the characteristic features of each design. Through a detailed analysis of pressure drop, surface area, and electrochemical behavior, we identified the diamond design as particularly effective in enhancing mass transport while maintaining low hydraulic resistance. We further assessed gyroid structures, selected for being the most well-known among TPMSs, across a range of porosities, finding that higher porosity improved flow performance despite a reduction in surface area, an advantageous trade-off for electrolytes with facile kinetics and low ionic conductivity. Comparison with a commercial carbon felt electrode revealed comparable ohmic resistance and favorable flow characteristics, though reduced electrochemical surface area limited the achievable current densities. To isolate mass transport effects, a kinetically facile organic redox couple was employed, after which a representative 3D-printed gyroid electrode was evaluated in a proof-of-concept full-cell vanadium redox flow battery. A full-cell test demonstrated the feasibility of printed electrodes, achieving a voltage efficiency of 76% at a current density of 50 mA cm−2. These findings demonstrate the potential of architected 3D printed electrodes for future redox flow batteries and highlight the importance of tuning geometry and porosity to balance power output, mass transport, and system-level pumping losses.
doi:10.1093/mtomcs/mfag032: Abstract Mercury toxicity is strongly influenced by its chemical speciation, with interactions between mercury and selenium species either mitigating or exacerbating toxic effects. Here, synchrotron-based X-ray fluorescence imaging was used to examine the influence of l-selenomethionine on the tissue distributions of inorganic mercury and methylmercury in zebrafish larvae. Inorganic mercury accumulated predominantly in the pronephric ducts and liver, whereas methylmercury was distributed more uniformly throughout the organism. Administration of l-selenomethionine substantially altered the distribution of inorganic mercury and increased selenium accumulation within the pronephric ducts. Subcellular-resolution imaging revealed strong spatial correlations among mercury, selenium, and sulfur following inorganic mercury exposure, revealing mercury-, selenium-, and sulfur-rich domains within the pronephric ducts. In contrast, l-selenomethionine had comparatively little influence on methylmercury distribution, although combined exposure increased tissue sulfur levels. These findings demonstrate fundamentally different interactions of selenium with inorganic and organometallic mercury species in vivo and emphasize the importance of both chemical form and subsequent metabolism in determining mercury–selenium interactions.
doi:10.21203/rs.3.rs-11257702/v1: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressively characterized neurodegenerative condition marked by molecular instability, neuronal dysfunction and abnormal tau buildup. Identification of disease-associated molecular signatures that can be experimentally validated in neuronal models may provide biologically relevant biomarkers and targets for therapeutic intervention. Here, we employed an integrated transcriptomic and cellular approach to identify and validate biomarkers associated with AD pathology. Differential transcriptomic analysis of (AD versus control) samples was used to prioritize candidate genes, followed by experimental validation in a streptozotocin (STZ) induced SH-SY5Y cells. Among the selected genes, anterior pharynx defective 1A (APH-1A) and cyclin dependent kinase (CDK5) were experimentally validated and further correlated to tau pathology by quantifying phosphorylation of tau at serine 396 (p-Tau Ser396) using confocal fluorescence microscopy. Complementary atomic force microscopy (AFM) was employed to characterize STZ-associated cellular morphological alterations. STZ exposure induced an AD-like neuronal phenotype characterized by associated cellular structural abnormalities. Importantly, co-treatment with (Brahmi) attenuated STZ-associated tau Ser396 phosphorylation and improved the cellular phenotype. The effects of Brahmi were further compared with those of established anti-Alzheimer’s drugs, Donep-M (Donepezil and Memantine) together, which similarly reduced p-Tau Ser396-associated alterations. The concordance between molecular biomarker validation and imaging-based phenotypic responses warrants further investigation of underlying molecular mechanisms. Collectively, our findings establish a transcriptome-to-cellular validation framework in which APH-1A and CDK5 represent experimentally supported AD-associated biomarkers. This integrated strategy provides a foundation for connecting human AD molecular signatures with measurable neuronal phenotypes and evaluating potential therapeutic interventions.
doi:10.1021/acs.nanolett.6c03022: Abstract RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.
doi:10.1002/nap2.70351: ABSTRACT Terahertz (THz) Airy beams hold significant promise for directional wireless links in future 6G communications. Unlike conventional phased arrays with high power consumption and complexity, metasurfaces offer a platform for flexibly tailoring the Airy beam. However, existing THz metasurface‐based Airy beam generators remain confined to one dimension, and experimental verification of their quasi‐nondiffracting and self‐healing characteristics is scarce. Here, we propose a composite bilayer metasurface for full‐space THz Airy beam manipulation and experimentally demonstrate its transmission channel capabilities. By varying the structural rotation angles, the metasurface enables linearly polarized (LP) amplitude‐phase and circularly polarized (CP) Pancharatnam‐Berry (PB) phase, switching between distinct transmission channels at 0.99 THz and reflection channels at 0.538 and 0.553 THz. Ring Airy beams (RAB), phase‐modulated ring Airy beams (PRAB), and elliptical Airy vortex beams (EAVB) are realized based on the proposed composite bilayer architecture. As proof‐of‐concept demonstrations, the prototypes of LP RAB and CP EAVB are fabricated and experimentally verified. The measured distributions show good agreement with simulations, confirming the ability of the metasurfaces to manipulate Airy beams across polarization states, frequencies, and transmission directions. This work provides a compact route toward multi‐dimensional THz Airy beam manipulation with broad application prospects in areas such as free‐space optical communications and 6G THz wireless communication.
doi:10.1021/jacs.6c08725: Abstract The microstructural properties of grain boundaries (GBs) and defects in semiconductor materials critically influence solar energy conversion. Yet, the precise role of GBs in charge separation and transport remains poorly understood and widely debated, particularly under reaction conditions. A key knowledge gap persists in linking charge separation and transfer to surface reactions at the GB-liquid interface, necessitating detailed operando nanoscale investigations. Here, we establish nanoscale, operando imaging of charge transfer and catalytic activity of a working BiVO4 photoanode using operando atomic force microscopy–scanning electrochemical microscopy (AFM-SECM) under illumination. We found distinct GB behaviors, with defect-rich GBs emerging as locally active regions for charge transfer and O2 generation, whereas other GBs impede charge transfer and serve as recombination sites. Specially for defect-rich GBs, operando electrochemical imaging and transient spectroscopy reveal that oxygen vacancies within GB interiors and on grain surfaces act synergistically on distinct time scales to trap photogenerated electrons and extend hole lifetimes into the millisecond range, thereby enhancing water oxidation activity locally at GBs. These insights underscore the pivotal role of defect-rich GBs in sustaining long-lived charge carriers, thereby highlighting the importance of modulating GB characteristics for efficient solar energy conversion.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79183-4: Achieving single-cell detection with electrochemical cytosensors remains challenging, owing to a poor understanding of how electroactive redox probes generate measurable signals near large, insulating cells. Here, we validate a cell–electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in situ visualizing that the measurable current signal originating from redox probes located at the cell–electrode adjacent interface, rather than from those distributed on the cell surface. Notably, cell spreading enlarges this cell-adjacent interface, thereby enabling effective current amplification. Guided by this effect, we design an integrated cytosensor platform that combines a highly conductive lamellar reduced graphene oxide (RGO)/Ti3C2Tx electrode chip, which facilitates lamellipodia-driven cell spreading, with a high peroxidase-activity FeCN single-atom nanozyme. This platform exhibits a 7.6-fold signal enhancement over conventional chips and a detection limit of 0.03 cells mL−1, allowing a resolvable current response from a single cell on the 2 cm2 large-sized chip. Furthermore, it demonstrates potential feasibility for clinical detection of circulating tumor cells, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity across 55 blood samples in distinguishing cancer patients from healthy controls. This work establishes a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer paradigm and advances electrochemical cytosensing toward high-performance liquid biopsy applications. Electrochemical cytosensors have emerged as powerful tools for single-cell analysis, but generating robust signals from individual cells remains a major challenge. The authors uncover a cell-electrode interfacial electron-transfer effect, in which only redox probes at the cell-electrode interface contribute to measurable currents. Exploiting this mechanism, they develop a cell spreading-enhanced electron-transfer (SEET) cytosensor and apply it to circulating tumor cell detection in 55 patient samples, achieving 96% specificity and 87% sensitivity.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79173-6: Abstract The morphology of the initial PbI 2 film is very pivotal in dictating the uniformity and crystallinity of the resultant perovskite film in the two-step sequential deposition processes. A solution-based induction is introduced to transform PbI 2 clusters into PbI 2 nanowires to achieve controllable morphology of the PbI 2 film. The nanowires act as scaffolds for the subsequent perovskite formation. An in-plane low-angle diffraction detected in the in-situ grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) for the PbI 2 film indicates the formation of a periodically arranged ordered structure. The PbI 2 nanowires facilitate the ion-exchange process, markedly improving the homogeneity and orientation of the perovskite films, which is confirmed by the in-situ grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As a result, a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.94% (certified as 26.66%, a very high certification efficiency of n-i-p structured perovskite devices) is achieved for the laboratory area (aperture area of the mask is 0.0618 cm 2 ). Moreover, a micro module device with an aperture area of 21.54 cm 2 was successfully manufactured and achieved a PCE of 24.60% (certified as 24.02%).
doi:10.1002/ange.1814901: ABSTRACT Lensless imaging offers a new route to substantially alleviate the shackle of space‐bandwidth‐product (SBP) on conventional optical microscopes, thus high resolution and wide field‐of‐view (FOV) can be more easily achieved simultaneously. A series of lensless imaging methods have taken their place in chemical bioimaging due to their advantages of wide FOV and low cost. This review discusses the development of sensor‐proximal contact, incoherent, holographic, and ptychographic imaging and evaluates their applications across cellular phenotyping, particle and molecular sensing, as well as tissue and in vivo imaging. Particular emphasis is placed on interfacial chemical strategies involving affinity reagents, responsive materials, luminescent reactions, and engineered probes. These approaches convert nanoscale chemical events, which cannot be directly resolved by lensless systems, into amplified and spatially resolved optical signals. By combining chemical signal transduction with large‐area imaging, lensless platforms can detect individual cells, particles, and molecular events while simultaneously capturing their temporal dynamics, spatial organization, and collective evolution. This chemistry‐centered minireview highlights future opportunities for extracting multiscale spatiotemporal information from complex chemical and biological systems.
doi:10.1007/s44371-026-01060-2: Abstract Polymeric nanocomposites (PNCs) are formed by dispersing fillers with at least one dimension in the 1–100 nm range in a polymer matrix, and the resulting materials often outperform either constituent alone. Because the interfacial area per unit volume scales inversely with the smallest filler dimension, a few volumes per cent of well-dispersed nanofiller can alter the mechanical, electrical, optical, magnetic and gas-barrier properties of the host polymer, at loadings substantially lower than those required with conventional micro-scale fillers. These benefits have attracted increasing attention from sectors such as water treatment, flexible electronics, aerospace shielding and food preservation. This review provides a thematically organised and critical overview of the PNC field. It first sets out the structure–property fundamentals (interfacial area, interphase volume, filler aspect ratio and dispersion state) that link nanoscale structure to macroscopic performance. It then compares four established fabrication routes (melt blending, in situ polymerisation, solution mixing and electrospinning) in terms of dispersion quality, interfacial bonding, scalability and environmental burden. Smart PNCs that respond to heat, light, electric and magnetic fields are compared with respect to mechanism, representative systems, advantages and limitations. The application sections compile quantitative data on dye and heavy-metal removal, sensing performance (detection limits and linear ranges), electromagnetic interference shielding effectiveness and shelf-life extension, and discuss safety, migration and regulatory requirements for food-contact and biomedical uses together with life-cycle considerations. Finally, the review identifies persistent bottlenecks (filler agglomeration, cost, reproducibility, toxicological uncertainty and regulatory gaps) and sets out research priorities, including scale-up, long-term durability, standardised testing and techno-economic assessment, that could accelerate responsible commercialisation.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79088-2: The sulfate formation from the residual SO2 in the industrial exhaust has long been recognized as the primary cause of sulfur poisoning for volatile organic compound oxidative removal. Contrary to the conventional understanding, here we show in situ sulfation enables dynamic activation of Pt1/MnxTi1-xO2 single-atom catalysts against sulfur poisoning, forming highly active Pt1/MnSO4 with Pt1-SO4 motif for excellent SO2-resistance in benzene oxidation. Utilizing state-of-the-art in situ characterizations and theoretical calculations, we identify two distinct sulfur species and their roles in reaction. The (SO3)ads adsorbates block Pt sites causing irreversible deactivation. In contrast, in situ sulfation promotes dynamic transformation of (SO3)ads into MnSO4, and enables Pt single-atom extraction to form Pt1-SO4 motif that prevents SO2 adsorption and preserves exposed Pt single-atom sites for benzene oxidation. This work provides dynamic insights for sulfation of Pt single-atom catalyst against SO2 poisoning and guides the general design of Pt1-SO4 motif for SO2 resistant oxidation. SO2 can deactivate catalysts used to remove harmful organic pollutants from industrial emissions. This study shows that sulfation instead creates active platinum sites that resist sulfur and sustain oxidation.
doi:10.29026/oet.2026.260024: The labile nature of conventional long-chain ligands on CsPbBr3 quantum dots (QDs) often leads to desorption during device fabrication, creating surface traps that compromise efficiency and stability. Here, we employ a supersaturation-precipitation method at room temperature, introducing 4-bromobutyric acid (BA) as a short-chain co-ligand alongside conventional oleic acid (OA) and oleylamine (OAm). The BA ligand anchors to surface Pb2+ via its carboxyl group, while its terminal Br− effectively fills surface Br vacancies. The combination of BA and OA enhances the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) to 84.96% and improves stability. density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed on CsPbBr3-OA, CsPbBr3-BA and CsPbBr3-OA/BA QDs to analyze charge density difference, density of states, and binding energy, demonstrating that BA can passivate surface defects, thereby enhancing the stability and photoluminescence (PL) performance of the materials. Single-particle spectroscopy shows that BA ligand engineering narrows the emission linewidth and prolongs the dephasing time of CsPbBr3 QDs, evidencing reduced local disorder and enhanced excitonic coherence. Coupled with a commercial 365 nm UV chip, green LED based on CsPbBr3-OA/BA QDs emits 1.42 times the PL intensity of CsPbBr3-OA ’s LED at 2.7 V. This work establishes short-chain ligands as an effective strategy to simultaneously achieve high efficiency and operational stability in perovskite QDs optoelectronics.

doi:10.1007/s44373-026-00183-6: Recently, lithium-ion capacitors (LICs) have emerged as a new energy-storage technology that combines the characteristics of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and supercapacitors. Their development has been driven by the growing demand for electrified transportation, stationary grid-storage systems, and portable electronic devices. In this review, recent advances in electrode materials and electrolyte chemistry, as well as interfacial phenomena for performance evaluation of LIBs and LICs, are discussed. Various carbon anodes and cathodes, transition metal oxides, phosphates, and chalcogenide-layered materials, as well as aqueous, nonaqueous, solid-state, and gel-polymer electrolytes used in LIBs and LICs are reviewed. Performance comparisons among electrode materials and full cells are presented, and the limitations of using metal electrodes, as well as strategies to improve them, are evaluated. The kinetic trade-off between the battery anode and the capacitor cathode, the balancing of electrode mass ratios, and the SEI/CEI interphases under high-voltage and high-rate regimes are considered in detail, along with recycling technologies and environmentally friendly synthesis routes for biomass-based electrode materials. Through systematic comparison of materials, mechanisms, performance, and degradation pathways, this review offers a practical approach to screening suitable electrode-electrolyte pairs for safer, more durable, and higher-performing future LIBs and LICs.
doi:10.1038/s44306-026-00163-x: Abstract The ever-increasing demand for fast, reliable, and energy-efficient information storage continues to push magnetic memory technologies toward their fundamental limits. Conventional scaling strategies, which rely on reducing bit size, inevitably run into the “magnetic recording trilemma,” where signal-to-noise ratio, thermal stability, and writability cannot all be optimized simultaneously. Heat-assisted magnetic recording (HAMR) has emerged as the leading solution, enabling high-density storage by transiently heating the medium during the write cycle. However, the reliance on laser optics and plasmonic transducers restricts HAMR primarily to hard-disk drives, limiting its integration with on-chip or embedded architectures. Here, we demonstrate an electronic variant of HAMR in which Joule heating from low-current density current pulses facilitates data writing, while the anomalous Hall effect provides electronic readout. Employing intercalated 2D magnet Ni 1/4 TaSe 2 , we show direct evidence that current pulses heat the material above its Curie temperature, during which a small magnetic field of 2 mT(100 times smaller than the coercive field) enables efficient data writing. The all-electronic approach combined with the 2D magnetic medium creates timely opportunities to revisit the energy-assisted magnetization recording, enabling new schemes that combine fundamental novelty with technological impact.
doi:10.1021/acsami.6c12166: Abstract The surface structure of semiconductor photocatalysts plays a critical role in the extraction of charge carriers during photocatalytic reactions. However, the surface structures of many photocatalysts are dynamic under catalytic conditions, which makes identifying photo-induced changes and their effect on photocatalytic activity challenging. Herein, we use super-resolution, single-molecule fluorescence imaging to map the spatial distribution of catalytically active regions and quantify the changes in activity of those regions for photocatalytic oxidation in bismuth titanium oxide (Bi4Ti3O12) nanoplates. Individual nanoplates varied widely in both activity and stability, reflecting significant heterogeneity among a single synthesis batch of photocatalyst particles. We observed that while the nanoplates are more active around the perimeter of the basal facet, those perimeter regions decrease in activity at the same relative rate as the rest of the basal facet, indicating a spatially uniform degradation mechanism. Through ensemble structural characterization of the nanoplates after irradiation, we identified surface hydroxyl groups as the photo-induced feature. Our results indicate that surface hydroxyl groups introduce hole trap states that increase charge recombination at the surface of the nanoplates, leading to the observed decrease in activity. Surprisingly, we identified nanoscale features that do not begin with high activity but exhibit a slower rate of activity loss, leading to regions with greater activity relative to the rest of the basal facet at the end of imaging. Our findings highlight the importance of not only understanding how different nanoscale features influence catalytic activity but also how these features evolve over time, which dictates catalyst stability.
doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78574-x: Conventional routes to strong protein fibers rely on the assembly of high-molecular-weight polymers, where mechanical performance is achieved by increasing the number of tandem repeats within the polypeptide chain. This repeat-number strategy inherently complicates production and limits scalability. Here, we introduce a contrasting paradigm in which macroscopic strength is derived not from chain length, but from the increased intrinsic mechanostability of each repeating unit. We implement this using computationally designed immunoglobulin-domain-based SuperMyo proteins, whose force-bearing β-strands are engineered to form ultra-dense hydrogen-bond networks, yielding unfolding forces nearly double those of natural immunoglobulin domains at a pulling speed of 1000 nm s−1. When assembled into minimal tetrameric constructs (only four repeats), these designed units retain their high nanomechanical stability. Processed via wet-spinning, the tetramers form continuous macroscopic fibers with a tensile strength up to 372 MPa and a toughness of 61 MJ m⁻³. Crucially, this performance matches or exceeds that of previously reported fibers spun from polymers containing far more repeats (e.g., 64-mers). Structural analyses confirm that the enhanced stability of the monomers promotes superior β-sheet crystallization and alignment during fiber formation. By demonstrating that engineering the mechanical stability of protein building blocks is a potential strategy for producing strong protein fibers from low-repeat-number constructs, this work establishes a more efficient and scalable foundation for manufacturing high-performance protein-based materials. High-performance biofuels require a well-defined flash point, yet the coexistence of pentanol isomers can introduce ignition-point variations that compromise fuel performance. Here, the authors present an electrochemiluminescence shunt strategy based on a bifunctional catalytic system that exploits the distinct reactive oxygen species scavenging properties of pentanol isomers. The approach generates differential anodic and cathodic luminol signals, enabling their precise discrimination and providing a powerful tool for fuel-quality assessment
doi:10.1021/acs.langmuir.6c06064: Abstract Eucalyptol (1,8-cineole) is a valuable bioactive monoterpene, but its volatility, water immiscibility, and chemical lability limit practical use. Here, we developed eucalyptol-in-water nanoemulsions stabilized by Pluronic F-127 and mapped their composition-dependent phase behavior, structure, and interfacial properties. A pseudoternary formulation map revealed a narrow window of transparent single-phase oil-in-water nanoemulsions, obtained at eucalyptol fractions of 0.01–0.04 (w/w) and Pluronic F-127 fractions up to 0.13 (w/w), whereas higher oil loadings promoted phase separation and excess polymer led to highly viscous or gel-like states. Dynamic light scattering showed nanodroplets with apparent hydrodynamic diameters of about 20–40 nm under optimal conditions, with droplet size increasing as eucalyptol content rose and a second smaller population appearing at higher polymer content, consistent with micellization and structural crowding. Conductivity increased with Pluronic F-127 content, while pH remained near 6.5–6.9 and zeta potential was essentially unchanged, confirming stabilization by a nonionic interfacial layer. Fluorescence spectroscopy indicated two eucalyptol environments, with emission bands centered near 310 and 325 nm, and increasing polymer content reduced fluorescence intensity through self-quenching. Contact angles on polystyrene averaged about 35°, independent of composition, whereas droplets spread almost immediately on glass. In a DPPH assay, nanoemulsions increased radical scavenging relative to free eucalyptol, although excessive Pluronic F-127 reduced this effect by densifying the interfacial shell. Overall, these results define the narrow but well-defined compositional window for carrier-oil-free, kinetically stable O/W eucalyptol nanoemulsions and reveal how oil–polymer interactions govern their formation, stability, and function.
doi:10.1186/s11671-026-04923-w: Abstract Infectious bone defects are a major challenge in orthopedics and stomatology, requiring strategies that eliminate bacteria and promote osteogenesis. Here, we developed a multifunctional composite magnetic particle system (F-Fe 3 O 4 ) and demonstrate its synergistic combination with a static magnetic field (SMF) for treating infectious bone defects. In vitro, F-Fe 3 O 4 demonstrated good biocompatibility with human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (hBMSCs) and facilitated their proliferation, migration, and osteogenic differentiation, while inhibiting the growth of Escherichia coli , Staphylococcus aureus , and Enterococcus faecalis . With the application with SMF, the aforementioned effects are further enhanced. The in vivo studies in the rat model further revealed that F-Fe 3 O 4 combined with SMF can reduce early infection, alleviate inflammation, and accelerate new bone formation. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing and verification experiments revealed that the combination therapy upregulated SLC2A1 -mediated glucose uptake and activated HIF-1 and PI3K/AKT signaling pathways, thereby enhancing the osteogenic differentiation of hBMSCs. In conclusion, this study developed an efficient treatment approach for infectious bone defects by integrating F-Fe 3 O 4 and SMF.

doi:10.25259/ajc_160_2026: Surfactant-enhanced oil recovery was an important technical direction for chemical enhanced oil recovery. It lowered the threshold for residual oil after water flooding and improved the micro-displacement efficiency and macro-development effects of complex reservoirs, which could be used to regulate the oil/water and oil/solid interface multiphase flow behavior. When the conventional reservoirs entered high water cut or recovery stages, the residual oil would gradually transformed from a continuous oil phase into the non-contiguous pore corner oil. But the residual oil flow was jointly limited by capillary pressure, rock surface adhesion, crude polar component aggregation, and interfacial film stability, and many methods (surfactants, polymers, ect) could be used to enhance the process. Among these methods, surfactants can be directionally adsorbed onto the oil-water interface to reduce the interface free energy, thus promoting the deformation, peeling and migration of oil droplets. At the same time, surfactants can form competitive adsorption layers or hydration films on the rock surface, altering the minerals suface wettability and chargeability. Additionally, surfactants can improve the crude oil mobility through emulsification and microemulsification‌. This paper reviewed the surfactant interfacial behavior onto the oil-water–rock interface, the surfactants species were analyzed, and the structural characteristics, interfacial interactions and reservoir suitability were analyzed. Surfactants could be divided into the cationic, anionic, non-ionic, and zwitterionic surfactant. Different surfactants had the different property onto the interface modification. The different surfactants application should mainly be limited to certain carbonate rock reservoirs, special surface electrical conditions, or composite systems modified by nonionic, amphoteric, and low-adsorption structures. This paper further clarifies the mechanisms of surfactant-intensified oil extraction, mainly focusing on processes such as reduced interfacial tension, changes in wetting properties, emulsification and formation of microemulsions, competition between adsorption and desorption, reconstruction of interfacial films, and transport of pore-scale dimensions. It also provides a detailed analysis of the effects of mineralization, divalent ions, temperature, pressure, rock mineral composition, and heavy crude oil components on interface behavior. doi:10.1002/adfm.79385: ABSTRACT The separator critically dictates liquid‐phase mass transport in aqueous zinc‐ion batteries (AZIBs), while it is poorly regulated in conventional commercial separators due to inappropriate pore structure and heterogeneous surface charge. Herein, we engineer a multifunctional separator (PTT‐GF‐D) that integrates ordered nanoporous channels with highly negatively charged surface to synchronously regulate ion flux and interfacial electric fields. This design effectively optimizes liquid‐phase mass transport, thereby promoting homogeneous multi‐site nucleation, accelerating Zn 2+ desolvation, and mitigating Zn 2+ concentration polarization. Consequently, the symmetric cells achieve exceptional reversibility, stably operating for 3300 h under 1 mA cm −2 , 1 mAh cm −2 and maintaining robust stability over 1000 h even under harsh conditions of 10 mA cm −2 , 10 mAh cm −2 . The as‐fabricated Zn||MnO 2 full cell delivers a specific capacity of 130 mAh g −1 at 1 A g −1 , preserving 96.2% of its initial capacity after 1000 cycles. A large‐sized pouch cell is also demonstrated, which can operate at 5 mA cm −2 for 100 cycles without noticeable decay. This study establishes the critical synergy of pore architecture and surface charge engineering in separators to control liquid‐phase mass transport, offering a promising strategy for developing high‐performance and practical AZIBs.
doi:10.1002/lpor.72130: ABSTRACT MXenes, a novel class of 2D transition metal carbides, carbonitrides, and nitrides derived from layered MAX phases, have attracted considerable attention for future photodetector applications due to their unique structural, optical, and electronic properties. Their tunable surface terminations (–O, –OH, –F) and metallic conductivity enable precise modulation of work function and carrier dynamics, facilitating efficient charge transfer and reduced dark current when integrated into semiconductor junctions. This review systematically explores the impact of various synthesis methods, such as HF, in situ HF, electrochemical, and alkali‐assisted etching, on MXene morphology, surface chemistry, and interfacial quality, which are critical for device performance. Key material properties relevant to photodetection, including optical transparency, high carrier mobility, tunable plasmonic response, and adjustable work function, are thoroughly examined. Furthermore, the review underscores MXene role in diverse photodetector designs, highlighting its application as an electrode, charge transport, and active‐layer material. By correlating synthesis techniques with intrinsic properties and device performance, this review provides a comprehensive understanding of how MXene engineering can enhance responsivity, detectivity, and spectral range in optoelectronic systems. Finally, it addresses the current challenges and future opportunities for optimizing MXene‐based materials for high‐performance, broadband, and flexible photodetectors.
doi:10.1016/j.sbi.2026.103424: With recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy/cryo-electron tomography (cryoEM/cryoET), computational capabilities and machine learning, there has been an incredible increase in the speed of structure determination for large biomolecular assemblies. In order to connect these static descriptions with biological function, one needs reliable and accurate approaches to quantify the factors that regulate dynamics. For this, models that employ simplified energetics and/or coarse-grained representations have become indispensable tools for integrating structural insights, biochemical analyses and physical principles. Here we discuss examples where molecular simulations have provided a framework for understanding dynamics in assemblies of increasing size and complexity. We focus on three classes for which there have been notable advances in recent years: ribosomes, viral capsids and nuclear pore complexes. Each possesses unique physical attributes that have required distinct theoretical and computational strategies. Together, these studies provide a rich conceptual and technical foundation that can help shape our perspective on the machinery of the cell.
